text:
The paper proposes an attention-based approach for video description. The approach uses three LSTMs and two attention mechanisms to sequentially predict words from a sequence of frames.

In the LSTM encoder of the frames (TEM), the first attention mechanism predicts spatial attention for each frame and computes a weighted average. The second LSTM (HAM) predicts attention over the hidden states of the encoder LSTM.

The third LSTM, which runs temporally in parallel with the second LSTM, generates the sentence one word at a time.

Strengths:
===============

- The paper works on a relevant and interesting problem.
- Using two layers of attention in the proposed way has, to my knowledge, not been used before for video description. The exact architecture is therefore novel, but the work claims much more without sufficient attribution; see below.
- The experiments are evaluated on two datasets, MSVD and Charades, showing performance at the level of related work for MSVD and improvements for Charades.

Weaknesses:
===============

1. Claims about the contribution and novelty of the model do not seem to hold:

1.1. One of the main contributions is the Hierarchical Attention/Memory (HAM):

1.1.1. It is not clear to me how the presented model (Eq. 6-8) is significantly different from the models in Xu et al. and Yao et al. While Xu et al. attend over spatial image locations and Yao et al. attend over frames, this model attends over encoded video representations h_v^i. A slight difference might be that Xu et al. use the same LSTM to generate, while this model uses an additional LSTM for decoding.

1.1.2. The paper states in Section 3.2, “we propose f_m to memorize the previous attention”; however, H_m^{t’-1} consists only of the last hidden state. Furthermore, the model f_m does not have access to the attention \alpha. This was also discussed in comments by others, but it remains unclear.

1.1.3. In the discussion of comments, the authors claim that “attention not only is a function a current time step but also a function of all previous attentions and network states.” While it is true that there is a dependency, this is also true for any LSTM. However, the model does not have access to the previous network states, as H_g^{t’-1} consists only of the last hidden state, as does H_m^{t’-1} [at least that is what the formulas say and what Figure 1 suggests].

1.1.4. The authors claim to have multi-layer attention in HAM, but it remains unclear where the multi-layer aspect comes from.

1.2. The paper states in Section 3.1 that “[CNN] features tend to discard the low level information useful in modeling the motion in the video (Ballas et al., 2016).” This suggests that the approach that follows addresses this problem. However, it cannot model motion, as attention \rho between frames is not available when predicting the next frame. Also, it is not clear how the model can capture anything “low level,” as it operates on rather high-level VGG conv5 features.

2. Related work: The difference between HAM and the models of Yao et al. and Xu et al. should be made clearer, or these papers should be cited in the HAM section.

3. Conceptual limitation of the model: The model has two independent attention mechanisms: a spatial one and a temporal one. The spatial attention within a frame is independent of sentence generation. It therefore cannot attend to different aspects of the frames for different words, which would make sense. For example, if the sentence is “the dog jumps on the trampoline,” the model should focus on the dog when saying “dog” and on the trampoline when saying “trampoline.” However, as the spatial attention is fixed, this is difficult. Also, the encoder model does not have an explicit way to look at different aspects of the frame during encoding, so it might likely get stuck and always predict the same spatial attention for all frames. Alternatively, it might always attend to the dog, which moves around, but never to the scene.

4. Eq. 11 contradicts Fig. 1: How exactly does the model receive the previous word as input? Eq. 11 suggests it is the softmax. If this is the case, the authors should emphasize this in the text, as this is unusual. More commonly, the ground-truth previous word would be used during training, which Fig. 1 suggests, and the “hardmax,” i.e., the highest predicted previous word encoded as a one-hot vector, would be used at test time.

5. Clarity:

5.1. It would be helpful if the same notation were used in Eq. 2-5 and Eq. 6-9. Why is different notation required?

5.2. It would be helpful if Fig. 1 contained more details, or if additional figures for the corresponding parts were added. If space is a problem, the well-known equations for the LSTM, softmax (Eq. 2), and log-likelihood loss (Eq. 12) could be omitted or inlined.

6. Evaluation:

6.1. The paper claims that “the proposed architecture outperforms all previously proposed methods and leads to a new state of the art results.”

6.1.1. For the MSVD dataset, this is clearly wrong, even given the same feature representation. Pan et al. (2016a) in Table 2 achieve higher METEOR (33.10).

6.1.2. For this strong claim, I would also expect the method to outperform all previous results independent of the features used, which is also wrong; Yu et al. achieve higher performance in all compared metrics.

6.1.3. For the Charades dataset, this claim is also too bold, as hardly any methods have been evaluated on this dataset. At least all the ablations reported in Table 1 should also be reported for the Charades dataset before making any stronger claims for this dataset.

6.2. Missing qualitative results of attention: The authors should show qualitative results of the attention for both attention mechanisms to help readers understand whether anything sensible is happening there. How diverse are the spatial and temporal attention? Are they peaky or rather uniform?

6.3. Performance improvement is not significant over model ablations: The improvement over Att+No TEM is only 0.5 METEOR and 0.7 BLEU@4, and the performance drops for CIDEr by 1.7.

6.4. Missing human evaluation: I disagree with the authors that a human evaluation is not feasible. First, an evaluation on a subset of the test data is not so difficult. Second, even if other authors do not provide their code or model [and some do], they are typically happy to share the predicted sentences, which is sufficient and even better for human evaluation. If not, I would explicitly mention that some authors did not share sentences, as this seems clearly wrong. Third, for model ablations, the sentences are available to the authors.

7. Several of the comments raised by reviewers or others have not yet been incorporated in a revised version of the paper and/or are still not clear from the explanations given. For example, including SPICE evaluation and making fixes seems trivial.

8. Hyperparameters are inconsistent: Why are the hyperparameters inconsistent between the ablation analysis, where 40 frames are sampled, and the performance comparison, where 8 frames are used? Should this not be selected on the validation set? What is the performance of all the ablations with 8 frames?

Other minor/discussion points:
===============

- Equation 10: What happens with h_m and h_g? The LSTM formulas provided handle only two inputs. Are h_m and h_g concatenated?
- There is a Section 4.1 but no Section 4.2.
- The paper states in Section 4.1 that “our proposed architecture can alone not only learn a representation for video that can model the temporal structure of a video sequence, but also a representation that can effectively map visual space to the language space.” However, this seems to be true also for many or most other approaches, e.g., Venugopalan et al. 2015 ICCV.

Summary:
===============

While the paper makes strong claims with respect to the approach and results, the approach lacks novelty and the results are not convincing compared with related work and ablations. Furthermore, improved clarity and visualizations of the model and attention results would benefit the paper.

text:
SUMMARY
This paper studies the expressive power of deep neural networks under various related measures of expressivity. It discusses how these measures relate to “trajectory length,” which is shown to depend exponentially on the depth of the network, in expectation (at least experimentally, at an intuitive level, or theoretically under certain assumptions). The paper also emphasizes the importance of the weights in the earlier layers of the network, as these have a larger influence on the represented classes of functions, and demonstrates this in an experimental setting.

PROS
The paper further advances topics related to the expressive power of feedforward neural networks with piecewise linear activation functions, in particular by elaborating on the relations between various points of view.

CONS
The paper further advances and elaborates on interesting topics, but in my appraisal it does not contribute significantly new aspects to the discussion.

COMMENTS
- The paper is a bit long, especially the appendix, and seems to have been written somewhat in a rush. Overall, the main points are presented clearly, but the results and conclusions could be clearer about the assumptions and about their experimental vs. theoretical nature. The connection to previous works could also be clearer.

- On page 2, one finds the statement: “Furthermore, architectures are often compared via ‘hardcoded’ weight values -- a specific function that can be represented efficiently by one architecture is shown to only be inefficiently approximated by another.”

This is partially true, but it neglects important parts of the discussion in the cited papers. In particular, the paper [Montufar, Pascanu, Cho, Bengio 2014] discusses not one hard-coded function, but classes of functions with a given number of linear regions. That paper shows that deep networks generically* produce functions with at least a given number of linear regions, while shallow networks never do.
*Generically means that, after fixing the number of parameters, any function represented by the network, for parameter values from an open, positive-measure neighbourhood, belongs to the class of functions that have at least a certain number of linear regions. In particular, such statements can be directly interpreted in terms of networks with random weights.

- One of the measures of expressivity discussed in the present paper is the number of dichotomies. In statistical learning theory, this notion is used to define the VC-dimension. In that context, a high value is associated with high statistical complexity, meaning that picking a good hypothesis requires more data.

- On page 2, one finds the statement: “We discover and prove the underlying reason for this – all three measures are directly proportional to a fourth quantity, trajectory length.”
The expected trajectory length increasing exponentially with depth can be interpreted as the increase (or decrease) in scale by a composition of the form a*...*a x, which scales the inputs by a^d. Such a scaling by itself certainly is not an underlying cause of an increase in the number of dichotomies, activation patterns, or transitions. Here it seems that at least the assumptions on the considered types of trajectories also play an important role. This is probably related to another observation from page 4: “if the variance of the bias is comparatively too large... then we no longer see exponential growth.”

OTHER SPECIFIC COMMENTS
In Theorem 1:
- It would be good to be more specific about “random neural network,” i.e., fixed connectivity structure with random weights, and also about the kind of one-dimensional trajectory, i.e., finite in length, closed, differentiable almost everywhere, etc.

- The notation “g \geq O(f)” used in the theorem reads literally as |g| \geq \leq k |f| for some k>0, for sufficiently large arguments. It could also be read as g being not smaller than some function that is bounded above by f, which holds, for instance, whenever g\geq 0. To express asymptotic lower bounds, one can use the notation \Omega (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation).

- It would be helpful to mention that the expectation is being taken with respect to the network weights and that these are normally distributed with variance \sigma.

- Theorem 2. It would be good to be more specific about the kind of sign transitions. Is this about transitions at any units of the network, or about sign transitions at the scalar output of the entire network?

- Theorem 3 is quite trivial. The bijection between transitions and activation patterns is not clear. Take a regular n-gon in the plane and a circle that crosses each edge twice. This makes 2n transitions but only n+1 activation patterns.

- Theorem 4. Where is the proof of this statement? How does this relate to the simple fact that each activation pattern corresponds to the vector indicating the units that are “active”?

MINOR COMMENTS
- The names of the theorems, e.g., “Bound on ...” in Theorem 1, could be separated more clearly from the statements, for instance by using bold font, a dot, or parentheses.
- On page 4, in LaTeX one can use \gg for the “much larger” symbol.
- On page 4, explain the notation \delta z_\orth.
- On page 4, explain that “latent image” refers to the image in the last layer.
- Why are there no error bars in Figure 2?
- On page 5, explain that the hyperplane is in the last hidden layer.
- On page 5, “is transitioning for any input.” This is not clearly stated, since a transition takes place at a point in a trajectory of inputs, not for a single input.
- The y-axis labels in Figure 1(c) and (d) are too small.
- Why are there no error bars in Figure 1(a) and (b)? The caption could at least mention that what is shown are the averages over experiments.
- In Figure 4(b), the curves are occluded by the labels.
- The numbering of results is confusing. In the appendix, some numbers are repeated from the main part, and some are missing.
- On page 19, Theorem 6. As far as I remember, Stanley also provides an elementary proof of the case with hyperplanes in general position. Many other works also provide elementary proofs using the same induction arguments in what is known as the sweep hyperplane method.

text:
The paper presents a method for training a generative model via an iterative denoising procedure. The denoising process is initialized with a random sample from a crude approximation of the data distribution and produces a high-quality sample via multiple denoising steps. Training is performed by setting up a Markov chain that slowly blends proposals from the current denoising model with a real example from the data distribution; using this chain, the current denoising model is updated toward reproducing the changed, “better” samples from the blending process.

This is a clearly written paper that considers an interesting approach to training generative models. I was intrigued by the simplicity of the presented approach and really enjoyed reading the paper.

The proposed method is novel, although it has clear ties to other recent work aiming to use denoising models for sampling from distributions, such as the work by Sohl-Dickstein and the recent work on using DAEs as generative models.

I think this general direction of research is important. The proposed procedure takes inspiration from the perspective of generating samples by minimizing an energy function via transitions along a Markov chain and, if successful, could potentially sidestep many problems of current procedures for training directed generative models, such as:
- convergence and mode coverage problems, as in generative adversarial networks
- problems with modeling multi-modal distributions, which can arise when a too-restrictive approximate inference model is paired with a powerful generative model

That being said, another method that seems promising for addressing these issues, and that also has some superficial similarity to the presented work, is the idea of combining Hamiltonian Monte Carlo inference with variational inference, as in [1]. As such, I am not entirely convinced that the method presented here will be able to perform better than the mentioned paper, although it might be simpler to train. Similarly, although I agree that using an MCMC chain to generate samples via an MC-EM-like procedure is likely very costly, I am not convinced such a procedure would not also work reasonably well for the simple MNIST example. In general, a more direct comparison between different inference methods using an MCMC-chain-like procedure would be nice to have, but I understand that this is perhaps outside the scope of this paper. One thing that I would have expected, however, is a direct comparison to the procedure from Sohl-Dickstein in terms of sampling steps and generation quality, as it is so directly related.

Other major points (good and bad):
- Although the method is generally explained well, some training details are missing. Most importantly, it is never mentioned how alpha or omega are set. I am assuming omega is 0.01, as that is the increase mentioned in the experimental setup. It is also unclear how alpha affects the capabilities of the generator. While it intuitively seems reasonable to use a small alpha over many steps to ensure slow blending of the two distributions, it is not clear how necessary this is or at what point the procedure would break. I assume alpha = 1 will not work, as the generator would then have to magically denoise a sample from the relatively uninformative draw from p0. The authors do mention in one of the figure captions that the denoising model does not produce good samples in only 1–2 steps, but that might also be an artifact of training the model with small alpha; at least, I see no a priori reason for this. More experiments should be carried out here.
- No infusion chains or generating chains are shown for any of the more complicated data distributions. This is unfortunate, as I feel these would be interesting to look at.
- The paper does a good job of evaluating the model with respect to several different metrics. The bound on the log-likelihood is nice to have as well.
- Unfortunately, the current approach does not come with any theoretical guarantees. It is unclear for what choices of alpha the procedure will work and whether there is some deeper connection to MCMC sampling or energy-based models. In my eyes, this does not subtract from the value of the paper, but it would perhaps be worth a short sentence in the conclusion.

Minor points:
- The second reference seems broken.
- Figure 3 starts at 100 epochs and, as a result, contains little information. Perhaps it would be more useful to show the complete training procedure and put the x-axis on a log scale.
- The explanation regarding the convolutional networks you use makes no sense to me. You write that you use the same structure as in the “Improved GANs” paper, which, unlike your model, generates samples from a fixed-length random input. I thus suppose you do not really use a generator with one fully connected network followed by up-convolutions, but rather have several stages of convolutions followed by a fully connected layer and then up-convolutions.
- The choice of parametrizing the variance via a sigmoid output unit is somewhat unusual. Was there a specific reason for this choice?
- Footnote 1 contains errors: “This allow to” -> “allows one to”; “few informations” -> “little information”; “This force the network” -> “forces the network.”
- Page 1 error: etc.
- Page 4 error: “operator should to learn”

[1] Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Variational Inference: Bridging the Gap, Tim Salimans, Diedrik P. Kingma, and Max Welling, ICML 2015

Copied here from my response below:

I believe the authors’ response clarifies all open issues. I strongly believe the paper should be accepted to the conference. The only remaining issue I have with the paper is that, as the authors acknowledge, the architecture of the generator is likely highly suboptimal and might hamper the performance of the method in the evaluation. This, however, does not at all subtract from any of the main points of the paper.

I am thus keeping my score as a clear accept. I want to emphasize that I believe the paper should be published, just in case the review process results in some form of cut-off threshold that is high due to overall “inflated” review scores.

text:
*** Paper Summary ***

The paper proposes a new neural network architecture. The layer weights of a classical network are computed as a function of a latent representation associated with the layer. Two instances are presented: (i) a CNN where each layer weight is computed from a lower-dimensional layer embedding vector; and (ii) an RNN where each layer weight is computed from a secondary RNN state.

*** Review Summary ***

Pros:
- I like the idea of bringing multiplicative RNNs and their predecessors back into the spotlight.
- LM and MT results are excellent.

Cons:
- The paper could be better written. It is too long for the conference format and needs refocusing.
- On related work, the relation to multiplicative RNNs and their generic tensor-product predecessors, Order 2 networks in C. Lee Giles’s definition, should be mentioned in the related work section. The differences from earlier research need to be explained and motivated. By the way, it is better to say that something is revisiting an old idea or training it at modern scale/on modern tasks than omitting it.
- On focus, it is not clear whether your goal is to achieve better performance or more compact networks. In the RNN section you lean toward the former; in the CNN section you seem to lean toward the latter.

I would suggest making the paper shorter and clearer, possibly leaving the CNN results for later publication. The relation to multiplicative/Order 2 networks and any differences need to be explained.

*** Detailed Review ***

Multiplicative networks are an extremely powerful architecture, and bringing them back into the spotlight is excellent. This paper has excellent results but suffers from poor presentation and a lack of clear focus. It spends time on details and omits important points. In its current form, it is much too long and is not self-contained without the appendices.

Spending more time on multiplicative RNNs and Order 2 networks at the beginning of the paper would be excellent. This would let you highlight the differences between this paper and earlier work. It would also be necessary to spend a little time on why multiplicative RNNs were used less than gated RNNs: it seems that the optimization problem involved in their training is trickier, and it would be helpful to explain whether you had a harder time tweaking optimization parameters or whether you needed longer training sessions compared to LSTMs or regular CNNs. On the name, I am not sure that “hypernetwork” helps the reader better understand the proposed architecture compared to multiplicative interactions.

In Section 3.2, you seem to imply that there are different settings of hypernetworks that allow one to vary from an RNN to a CNN. This is not clear to me; maybe you could show how this would work on a simple temporal problem with equations.

The work on CNNs and RNNs seems rather disconnected to me. For CNNs, you seem to be interested in a low-rank structure of the weights, showing that similar performance can be achieved with fewer weights. It is not clear to me why you pursue that goal. Do you expect speedups? Less memory for embedded applications? In that case, you should compare with alternative strategies, e.g., model compression (Caruana et al. 2006, aka Dark Knowledge, Hinton et al. 2014) or hashed networks (Chen et al. 2015).

For RNNs, you seem to target better perplexity/BLEU, and model compactness is not a priority. Instead of making the weights have a simpler structure, you make them richer, i.e., dependent over time. It seems that, in this case, models might be bigger and take longer to train. You might want to comment on training time, inference time, and memory requirements in that case, as you highlight that this might be an important goal in the CNN section. Overall, I am not sure it helps to have this mixed message. I would rather see the paper fit in the conference format with the RNN results alone and a clearer explanation, deferring publication of the CNN results until a proper comparison with memory-focused methods is performed.

Some of the discussions are not clear to me. I am not sure what message the reader should get from Figure 2 or from the discussion of saturation statistics (p. 10, Figure 5). Similarly, I am not sure whether Figure 4 is showing anything: everything should change more drastically at word boundaries even in a regular LSTM, since states and gate units should look very different before and after a space. Without such a comparison, it is hard to see whether this is unique to your network.

The results on handwriting generation are harder for me to compare. Log-loss values are hard to understand, and I have no sense of whether the difference between models is significant. What would be the variance in this metric under bootstrap sampling of the training set? I am not sold either on a qualitative metric where humans can assess quality but cannot evaluate whether the network is repeating the training set. Did you think about a precision/recall metric for ink, possibly with some spatial tolerance, e.g., as in evaluation of segmentation tasks in vision?

The MT experiments are insufficiently discussed in the main text.

Overall, I would suggest making the paper shorter and clearer, possibly leaving the CNN results for later publication. You need to properly discuss the relation to multiplicative/Order 2 networks and highlight the differences. Unclear discussion can be eliminated to make the experimental setup and the results presentation clearer in the main text.

*** References ***

M.W. Goudreau, C.L. Giles, S.T. Chakradhar, D. Chen, “First-Order Vs. Second-Order Single Layer Recurrent Neural Networks,” IEEE Trans. on Neural Networks, 5 (3), p. 511, 1994.

Cristian Bucila, Rich Caruana, and Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil, “Model Compression,” The Proceedings of the 12th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD-2006), August 2006, pp. 535–541.

Dark Knowledge, G. Hinton, O. Vinyals, J. Dean, 2014.

W. Chen, J. Wilson, S. Tyree, K. Weinberger, and Y. Chen, “Compressing Neural Networks with the Hashing Trick,” Proc. International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML-15).

text:
Overview

This book chapter overviews what motivates different types of mindsets. From reading this chapter, you should gain knowledge about mindsets, including their definition, types of mindsets, causes of these mindsets, and related concepts. From there, this chapter will emphasise what motivates people to have the type of mindset they possess and how to alter it.

What is a mindset?

"When you are faced with a challenging task, do you a) complete the task, or b) watch a TV show? Your answer to this is determined by your mindset" (Steverink & Lindenberg, 2006).

A mindset is a frame of mind, or a set of beliefs, thoughts, or self-perceptions that humans possess (De Young, 1986). This can determine an individual's situation, mental attitude, and behaviour. For example, a mindset of "I am not good at playing the piano" will result in the behaviour of not playing the piano. However, a mindset of "I haven't learnt how to play the piano properly yet" is more likely to result in practising the piano until the individual becomes good at playing the piano (Krakovsky, 2008).

The term mindset was first identified by Stanford University psychologist Carol Dweck. Dweck argues that individuals obtain their abilities from a variety of beliefs they hold (Mercer & Ryan, 2009). Dweck found these beliefs to be based around either a fixed mindset or a growth mindset (Krakovsky, 2008).

Fixed mindset

A fixed mindset is where individuals believe qualities such as talent or intelligence are traits people are born with. This fixed mindset leads individuals to view their intelligence and talents as fixed and to spend less time developing these qualities (Cecere, Mancinelli, S & Mazzanti, 2014). A person with this type of mindset believes that effort is not required to pursue success or be successful, as the talent and intelligence they were born with create either success or failure (Mercer & Ryan, 2009).

People with a fixed mindset typically describe themselves as "intelligent" or "dumb" and will not do anything to change these abilities (Govindarajan & Gupta, 2009). When these people are faced with a challenge or failure, they tell others and themselves that they are unable to accomplish it, or they create other excuses to explain their failure (e.g., "I failed the exam because I was busy studying for another unit and didn't have enough time to study for this exam"). This is because their egos are easily threatened, and they have a need to prove themselves (Cecere, Mancinelli, S & Mazzanti, 2014).

text:
Overview

“Why don’t people change? Do people fail to see how serious the situation is? Do they not have enough knowledge to understand that certain bad habits are destroying their health? Or do they simply not care?”

Many health professionals ponder such questions when trying to help patients in a health crisis change their behaviour. But hesitancy to change is part of human nature (Hettema, Steele & Miller, 2005). Clients who present to health clinics for help exhibit a wide range of readiness (Miller & Rollnick, 2013). Eight out of ten people in need of change are ambivalent about change (Miller & Rollnick, 2013).

According to Prochaska and Diclemente’s transtheoretical model, behaviour change encompasses a cycle of stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance. At the precontemplation and contemplation stages, people often think about change, but they do not act. The primary goal for therapists, then, is to help clients overcome the hurdle of hesitation and move in the direction of change (Hettema et al., 2005; Miller, 2004).

This chapter discusses how to use motivational interviewing (MI) to resolve ambivalence toward change and thereby elicit behaviour change. It will begin by explaining what MI is, its underlying theories, and its real-world applications, especially in health care settings.

What is MI?

MI is a client-centred counselling style used to enhance personal motivation for behaviour change by exploring and overcoming ambivalence (Miller, 2004). It was originally designed as a prelude to be integrated with other clinical methods to assist clients through motivational obstacles to change (Miller, 2004). It can also be delivered as a brief stand-alone intervention, usually in one or two sessions (Hettema et al., 2005). Based on the transtheoretical model of change, MI aims to prepare clients to shift from precontemplation and contemplation to the real stage of change (Miller & Rollnick, 2009). Clients who are ready for change are unlikely to benefit from MI. Clients who appear to be angry, resistant, and less ready for change seem to benefit most from MI (Miller & Rollnick, 2009).

The beauty of MI is that it selectively reinforces clients’ own reasons for change, almost as if clients talk themselves into change (Miller & Rollnick, 2009). A skilful therapist walks with the client along a road from initial ambivalence to motivational readiness, an achievable plan for change, and commitment to the change (Miller & Moyers, 2006). Therefore, MI encompasses two phases: stimulating motivation for change and reinforcing commitment to change (Miller & Rollnick, 2009).

Overview

When Debra was 19 years old, she was admitted to a mental health centre. She weighed 29 kilos. Her liver, pancreas, and kidneys were damaged, and she spent almost two months in hospital recovering. During this time, Debra received psychotherapy that helped her understand why her eating behaviour had become dangerous. She also engaged in a behaviour modification program that rewarded her with privileges for each kilo she gained. Slowly, she began to gain weight and, through therapy, developed a clearer understanding of her eating behaviour. When she left the hospital, she weighed 48 kilos, and two years later, she was maintaining a steady weight (Steele, 1977).

Debra's experience highlights the burden of anorexia, a debilitating eating disorder that leads to diminished quality of life and serious adverse health effects. It is a complex disorder and has been the focus of research attempting to determine contributing factors and effective treatments. It also lends itself to many questions: What motivates an individual to engage in damaging eating habits? Are internal or external motivations responsible?

This chapter examines the external motivational factors that contribute to the development of anorexia. It will also attempt to answer some of the questions above and, hopefully, answer your own questions; so if you have any, keep them in mind while you read.

Eating disorders

Eating disorders are characterised by persistent disturbance surrounding eating or eating-related behaviours, leading to significant psychological distress, impaired functioning, and, in some cases, death (APA, 2013). It is estimated that approximately 4% of the Australian population has an eating disorder (Butterfly Foundation, 2016), with at least 15% of women experiencing an eating disorder at some point in their lives (NEDC, 2016). Some common eating disorders are listed in Table 1. Eating disorders are diagnosed in Australia through the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, fifth edition, a clinical tool that lists currently recognised mental disorders and includes information about the different subtypes, causes, and prevalence of these disorders (APA, 2013).

Table 1. Summary of common eating disorders

Note: An individual may have problems or issues surrounding eating and eating behaviours, but these will only fall under the definition of an "eating disorder" if they cause significant impairment in that individual's life. For example, Eddie may be very focused on eating only vegetables and doing at least two hours of exercise every day, but until these behaviours start to interfere with other aspects of Eddie's life, he would not be diagnosed with an eating disorder (APA, 2013).

text:
Overview

It’s the night before your big presentation! You’re nervous. Sleep won’t come as you toss and turn, mulling over your speech. “Is it good enough?” “What if I stumble over my words?” “What will everyone think of me?”

Morning finally arrives; butterflies are plaguing your stomach. Your heart is racing, and your hands tremble as you slowly step up onto the stage. All eyes are on you! You brace yourself and take a huge breath before you begin.

Have you ever experienced this scenario or something similar? You are not alone! In fact, public speaking anxiety is one of the most prevalent fears in the general population (Geer, 1995; Stein, Walker & Forde, 1996). The experience can affect anyone, with epidemiological studies demonstrating that prevalence is not dependent on gender, ethnic group, or age (Osorio et al., 2008). Numerous studies have found that fear of public speaking is more common, and rated more highly, than fear of death (Jagdag & Balgan, 2015). Comedian Jerry Seinfeld highlighted this astonishing finding in one of his stand-up routines:

“According to most studies, people’s number one fear is public speaking—number two is death. Death is number two? Does that seem right? To the average person, that means that if they have to go to a funeral, they’d be better off in the casket than giving the eulogy.” —Jerry Seinfeld (1993)

So why does this fundamental social skill make us so anxious? Why does our body shift into fight-or-flight mode in response to something that poses no real threat? Although there may not be a physical threat associated with public speaking, there is a psychosocial one. When we engage in public speaking, in some respects, our reputation, competence, and intelligence are all put under the microscope. If we mess up, what will everyone think? As social animals, the opinions of others matter greatly to us. Giving a great talk has the potential to inspire others, increase our social status, get us promoted, or convey insight on a revolutionary topic. A poor speech, however, is often accompanied by pity, embarrassment, and an attack on our competency. The prospect of these negative consequences has the potential to send us into a sort of “emergency mode.” The following chapter will attempt to explain why some of us enter this state of emotional emergency, as well as offer advice on how to manage the fear and anxiety associated with public speaking.

Overview

Imagine two children, Tim and Sam, learning to play field hockey. Both boys want to play for Australia one day.

Let's assume that both are equally talented. They improve in skill at the same rate, proportional to their training intensity.

The only obvious difference between the two boys is the duration and direction of their effort (Figure 1).

Sam doesn't practice between training sessions. He finds it tedious, and he plays two other sports. Tim, on the other hand, is passionate about hockey. He spends most days practising ball skills, having specialised running training, or watching the senior teams play. Tim has decided to deepen his understanding of the game and apply long-term effort to playing hockey.

Which one is more likely to be successful?

According to the Oxford Dictionary (2016), the simple meaning of the quality known as “grit” is “courage and resolve; strength of character.” This definition focuses on what could be described as positive, and even socially desirable, virtues that suggest a sense of nobility in a “gritty” individual. However, this simple definition does not capture the driving force behind grit, nor the end state toward which it directs effort.

This chapter explores grit as a personality trait driven by passion for a specific long-term goal (Duckworth, 2007). Differences between grit and other qualities, such as perseverance, hardiness, resilience, and conscientiousness, will be considered, as well as psychological theories relevant to achievement: need for achievement (McClelland, 1961), self-efficacy (Bandura, 1977), Self-Determination Theory (SDT: Deci & Ryan, 2000), and achievement goals theory (Senko, Hulleman, & Harackiewicz, 2011).

The benefits of being “gritty” will also be discussed before looking at the potential to develop grit in individuals through fostering a growth mindset (Dweck, 2015) and embracing positive psychology principles (Kobau et al., 2011; Seligman & Csikszentmihalyi, 2000).

Definition

What is “grit”?

Contemporary grit researcher Angela Duckworth, with colleagues Peterson, Matthews, and Kelly (2007, p. 1087), defines grit as “perseverance and passion for long-term goals.” These authors note that gritty individuals approach, rather than avoid, challenges and maintain effort and interest in their goals over years, regardless of setbacks, periodic boredom, or adversity.

Duckworth et al. (2007) found that grit accounted for more variance in success outcomes than could be explained by IQ or by the Big Five personality factor of conscientiousness. They also found that older individuals tended to have more grit than their younger counterparts, suggesting that this quality may increase with life experience. Importantly, they stress that grit is not just about working harder, but about working longer without switching objectives.

text:
Overview

In the technology world today, electronics are constantly developing (Huang & Yang, 2010). The internet now allows consumers to shop conveniently anywhere and anytime via any available tablet or device on hand. Online shopping has become a common way for shoppers to purchase a variety of goods, products, and services in an environment that supports privacy and confidentiality (Amin, B. & Amin, P., 2013). It enables online consumers to search for and control information or messages about what can be seen and heard by others (Amin, B. & Amin, P., 2013). Many researchers have explained internet purchase behaviour by identifying conceptual factors through the exploration of motivations (Huang & Yang, 2010). However, not many online purchase motivations have been examined (Huang & Yang, 2010). This book chapter will discuss motivations that may cause online shopping behaviour.

Personality Traits

In various contexts, personality traits may be a source of motivation (Huang & Yang, 2010). The Big Five has been used to select employees and determine work performance; however, its impact on online shopping motivations has not been properly examined (Huang & Yang, 2010). Studies on online gaming have shown a link between the Big Five traits and motivations (Huang & Yang, 2010). Therefore, factors that influence online shopping behaviour may also be determined by testing the relationship between personality traits and individual motivations (Huang & Yang, 2010).

The Big Five Model

The Big Five Model of personality traits includes openness, agreeableness, extraversion, conscientiousness, and neuroticism. Openness represents curiosity and creativity (Boundless, 2016). Individuals with high levels of agreeableness tend to be compassionate, considerate, generous, and cooperative towards others (Boundless, 2016). Extraversion consists of positivism, assertiveness, sociability, and talkativeness (Boundless, 2016). Conscientious individuals tend to show self-discipline, are organised and dependable, and are prepared and able to plan ahead for the future (Huang & Yang, 2010). Neuroticism refers to showing negative emotions such as anger, depression, and anxiety in stressful situations, and may be known as emotional stability (Boundless, 2016).

Motivations

Five internet shopping motivations associated with the Big Five personality traits have been selected for examination (Huang & Yang, 2010). These include adventure, idea, sociality, lack of sociality, and convenience (Huang & Yang, 2010). Adventure has been defined as encountering something interesting while experiencing joy during shopping (Huang & Yang, 2010). Idea refers to online shoppers being able to search for and understand information about product brands and new trends while experiencing pleasure (Huang & Yang, 2010). Sociality indicates that shoppers are able to socialise with other shoppers who have the same interests and share information (Huang & Yang, 2010). Lack of sociality describes shoppers not needing to bargain with sales assistants or waste the time of their companions (Huang & Yang, 2010). Convenience may represent a convenient and relaxing environment for shoppers without time, space, or weather issues (Huang & Yang, 2010).

text:
Overview

Positive emotions enable us to achieve higher functioning. Happiness is not only the result of hard work and success; it is also present before we experience our greatest achievements or moments of higher functioning. Positive emotions build an individual’s long-term psychological, intellectual, social, and physical well-being and resources (Fredrickson, 2004). They are the building blocks that help people become the best version of themselves, supporting them as they learn, grow, thrive, and maintain a higher level of life satisfaction.

To help explain the effect positive emotions have in a person’s life, Barbara Fredrickson developed a theory showing how people’s minds are broadened through experiencing positive emotions. The Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions suggests that positive emotions broaden a person’s awareness and encourage exploratory thoughts and actions. In light of the discoveries made by Fredrickson and other positive psychologists, this chapter will focus on the Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions: what it is, how it can be applied to everyday life, the benefits of feeling good, and some of the theory’s limitations.

Finding ways to be satisfied and happy with life is important, and it is something many people do not realize can be changed if they dedicate enough time and awareness to it.

A question you can ask yourself while reading this chapter is:

What is the Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions?

Several studies have examined the impact of positive emotions, but they have not fully captured the unique effects these emotions have on our emotional and physical well-being and functioning. In light of this, Fredrickson (2004) developed an alternative model designed to capture the significant impact positive emotions have on our daily lives, called the Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions.

It has been shown that positive emotions broaden people’s momentary thought-action repertoires and build their enduring personal resources (Fredrickson, 1998, 2001). The Broaden-and-Build Theory describes the form and function of a subset of positive emotions, such as joy, interest, contentment, and love. These positive emotions have a complementary effect and, compared with neutral states, widen the variety of thoughts and actions that come to a person’s mind.

For example, when someone is feeling joyful, this creates an urge to play, push their comfort zone, be impulsive, and be creative—not only in social and physical behaviour, but also intellectually, in intimate relationships, and artistically (Fredrickson, 2004). Similarly, when a person is feeling interested, this can create an urge to explore, take in new information and experiences, and expand their sense of self through the process of developing and adopting these new interests.

Contentment is the third distinct positive emotion. It elicits the urge to sit back and appreciate current life circumstances and integrate this appreciative nature into new views of the self and beliefs about the world (Fredrickson, 2004). Finally, love, which is viewed as a combination of all the distinct positive emotions mentioned, is experienced within a person’s safe, intimate relationships. It nurtures a person by creating a recurring cycle of the urges produced by joy, interest, and contentment.

Overview
Affective forecasting can influence motivation and decision making (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). Often, affective forecasting is inaccurate, largely due to three factors: impact bias, focalism, and immune neglect. These inaccuracies are referred to as affective forecasting errors, which can affect the likelihood of behaviour occurring.

Appraisal theory states that emotions occur as a result of an assessment of a situation or stimulus. Once an emotion is apparent, the behavioural response to that emotion is then expressed. Research on affective forecasting is somewhat limited and should be further investigated, especially in consideration of the impact that appraisals of future emotional states have on decision making.

Affective Forecasting
Affective forecasting occurs when people make predictions about what they anticipate their emotional reactions will be to future events (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). There are three main factors that contribute to affective forecasting errors: impact bias, focalism, and immune neglect (Halpern & Arnold, 2008).

Impact Bias
Impact bias occurs when people overestimate the intensity and/or duration of emotional affect in response to an event (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). The problem with the incorrect assumption that an event will be more emotionally evocative is that decision making regarding that event is subsequently affected (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). Classical and operant conditioning persuade us to repeat or cease behaviours depending on their expected result (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). This is also true of expected emotional outcomes. If a person expects to be rewarded with a happy emotional state after an event, they are more likely to attend. Conversely, if they expect to be made angry or upset by an event, they will likely try to avoid it (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005).

Focalism
Focalism refers to a person’s failure to anticipate other co-occurring factors that may influence or contribute to their emotional experience of a future situation (Emanuel, Updegraff, Kalmbach, & Ciesla, 2010). An example of this is die-hard sports fans who overestimate the elation they would experience if their team won the grand final (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). In reality, there are an abundance of factors that could diminish their overall positive experience of the good result (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005). They could be stressed by work, have just broken up with their partner, have lost a loved one, and so on, all of which could detract from their happiness about their team winning (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005).

Immune Neglect
People often underestimate their capacity to cope with, adapt to, and understand emotional situations and their responses to them (Halpern & Arnold, 2008). Coping and defence mechanisms are often largely unconscious processes that occur without active consideration (Halpern & Arnold, 2008). People make sense of their emotions and feelings in a way that accelerates their emotional recovery, often much faster than they tend to anticipate (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005).

text:
Overview

A long-term goal is a goal that is achieved over a long period of time. According to the Fare Fax dictionary, long-term goals are “goals that are the ultimate result desired when a plan is established or revised” (Miller-Keane, 2003). This definition suggests that this type of plan requires a certain level of motivation and passion, as well as a particular level of mastery of the task or activity. This chapter focuses on long-term goals and the effects that motivation and goal-setting theories have on the likelihood of completing goals.

The study of goal setting began in the late 1800s as an attempt to improve work productivity (Latham & Locke, 2007). However, it was not until the 1960s that Edwin Locke pioneered the study of goal setting and began to develop a theory. Gary Latham also began work on goal setting, and in the late 1990s the two published the first theory of goal setting. They identified that long-term goals could be achieved by following five key steps. They discovered that, for a goal to be achievable over a long period of time, it needs to be specific and difficult. Further scholars (*add their references here*) extended Locke and Latham’s theory, discovering that goals also need to include an element of feedback, that goals need to be achievable or broken down into smaller tasks or activities, and that the goal setter must be committed or driven by intrinsic motivation. While Locke and Latham’s theory pioneered scholarship on goal setting, it fails to account for the differences in motivation that people have for setting long-term goals in the first place. An additional theory called “grit” addresses such differences in motivation. Grit theory specifically considers how different personalities can affect a person’s ability to successfully complete long-term goals and further highlights the importance of motivation in long-term goal achievement.

Learning outcome

This chapter aims to inform the reader about the following:

Why is it important?

Many scholars have said that setting goals is linked to success (Locke, Latham, 2003; Jung, 2014; Gbadmosi, 2009; Duckworth et al., 2007). For example, Jung (2014) highlights that setting goals improves staff turnover, increases productivity, and reduces workplace boredom. Goal setting has also been shown to enhance a person’s perception that their job is important and to improve overall job satisfaction (Jung, 2014).

Cognitive dissonance is the feeling someone gets when a person holds two or more pieces of knowledge that are relevant, but not consistent, with one another (Gbadamosi, 2009). This dissonance, or conflict, creates mental strain as the person tries to make sense of these separate pieces of information (Gbadamosi, 2009). In relation to goal setting, people can experience a similar feeling of conflict when they want to change a current behaviour, action, or personality trait into one that is desired but, as yet, unrealised because it exists in the future. In order to remove this discrepancy between the person you are and the person you want to become, a person can do one of two things: either they can change their ideals to match their current abilities, or they can actively change themselves by setting challenging yet specific long-term goals.

Has anyone else had similar issues, and how did you cope?

For years, I worked on an ambitious sci-fi/fantasy project. I guess I still am; I definitely want to finish it. But I couldn’t write it regularly. The writer’s block was constant, perhaps because of the pressure I was putting on myself.

I solved the problem by accident. I played League of Legends, a video game with truly derpy lore that still had some cartoony charm. I started a community for roleplaying and themed matches, and wrote filler fanfic/fanlore to add flavor to the competitions. People enjoyed it, so I kept going. It was easy because my attitude was, “Whatever, just write something. It doesn’t have to be perfect; it’s just for a silly game.”

Over time, I found myself almost unconsciously trying to make that throwaway lore good. More than a year in, I realized I was writing regularly. It was very Zen: I only succeeded when I “gave up.”

This is just a start, but after years of procrastination and angst, I’m pleased I’ve begun in earnest. Like so many real authors say: you’ve just got to write.

Had I known at the beginning what I was in for, I might never have started. I’ve written three drafts, and my novel has evolved in completely unexpected ways. I cut scenes I thought would be critical, while sections I added on a whim became some of the novel’s best.

Looking back at the first scenes I wrote, I can see how much I’ve grown. My voice is stronger now, and my dialogue is much better. The book alternates among five viewpoints, so in some ways it felt like writing five separate novels. One character was especially difficult; I rewrote her arc three or four times, and now she is one of my favorites.

Next, I need beta readers, and then an agent. For now, I want to savor the victory.

Edit: Thank you for the kind words and encouragement. The working title is Revolutions! Pole Fitness for Women, a 125,000-word literary/women’s fiction novel about Corine, a pole-fitness studio owner, and her level-one students, whose expectations about pole dancing are overturned.

The contract hasn’t been finalized yet, so I can’t name names or tell anyone I know until Monday, when I can sign. But my agent just called, and I had to tell someone.

I started writing seriously at 38 while teaching, which is still my day job and first love. My first manuscript sucked, though I couldn’t see it then. My second sucked in different ways. My third was almost good enough, and my fourth was ready for readers, though it was in a genre that wasn’t selling; five agents said they loved it but couldn’t find a home for it.

So I wrote my fifth manuscript—this one. On my 37th query, I signed with an agent at a boutique agency. We revised it and sent it out in June. Nothing. In December, we tried a second round: love from editors, but not acquisitions teams.

Then an editor from the first round loved it. Fifteen months later, two weeks before my 45th birthday, she made an offer. I’m accepting, and next year I may see it on bookstore shelves.

After reading a bunch of threads on /r/FanTheories, I thought about the plot for the novel I'm writing and started considering whether there were any scenarios ambiguous enough to allow for that kind of interpretation.

I started thinking along the lines of “what if this was really that?” or “what if this character wasn’t trying to do this, but actually that?” and realised there was room for a huge underlying conspiracy that drastically alters the dynamic of the story while keeping all the plot details completely intact. I had worried my plot was too linear, but now I'm finding so much room for depth where I'd previously felt there was none.

Maybe it's just the coffee or how late it is here, but this felt like such a eureka moment that I thought I'd share it. It probably won't work for every plot, but the way this one just fell into place was so wonderfully satisfying, and even a bit mind-blowing, that I'd recommend it to anyone who isn't 100% sure of their plot.

Many an excited scribble tonight.

Edit: This got more attention than I expected! I hope the people who've read this get as much joy from the idea as I did.

text:
My novel-in-progress had gone untouched for a very long time. Somewhere between work, college, and dating, I became very disillusioned with the writing process and just couldn't bring myself to care anymore.

Tuesday morning, I decided on a whim to go back and read over some of the 100-ish pages I'd written before I had to go to work. This was after barely opening the document at all in two years. I thought about it through the whole first half of my shift and started adding more to it on my lunch break. I went home and continued working on it.

Now it's Friday night, and I've added over 30,000 words that I'm really, really happy with. I know that isn't very much in the grand scheme of things, and probably isn't all that impressive to people who actually write on a consistent basis like I want to. But I'm proud of it, and I wanted to come here and brag a little. Thanks for reading!

text:
Hello everyone.

Last year, I self-published a book about my attempt to get really good at playing table tennis.

It did “well” in the sense that it topped some Amazon best-seller lists and remained near the top for the rest of the year. It’s currently still #1 on the USA Amazon Kindle table tennis best-seller list.

But despite that, sales haven’t been great.

In the last year, it has sold:

Paperback: 443 copies — £1,665.39 (~$2,200)
Kindle: 429 copies — £1,003.46 (~$1,400)
Audiobook: 82 copies — £405.57 (~$550)

To be honest, I thought there would be a lot more demand. I got pretty excited when I saw the best-seller tag, then quickly deflated after checking the sales figures.

To the more experienced writers here, how does this compare with your experiences?

If you’re interested in a more detailed breakdown of how the year went, you can check out my post on it.

text:
# A gem of a book!

It is beginning to be some years since I last read Emile Ajar’s lovely novel *The Life Before Us*.

Now the book has appeared in a new edition from the publisher Agora Publishing (with the same translation as the original Norwegian edition from 1976 — Anne Elligers’s), which, in cooperation with Aschehoug Publishing, aims to “publish some of the most significant foreign writers of our time in Norwegian translation,” “... most of them ... already well established on the international literary scene,” to quote from an article about the launch of the publishing house on Aschehoug’s website. Agora Library, in other words, consists of a selection of exquisite literature, and it is the writer Gabi Gleichmann who is the editor of the editions.

The man behind the pseudonym Emile Ajar is Romain Gary (b. 1914 d. 1980). He published quite a number of books during his writing career — about 40. There is a rather special story behind his choice to publish some books under the pseudonym Emile Ajar. Allegedly, he was tired of himself, and through this pseudonym got the opportunity to be a spectator to his other life. That it was he who was behind the novel *The Life Before Us* did not become known until some time after he had won the Goncourt Prize for the book, more precisely after he had taken his own life in 1980. He was originally from Lithuania and was not even named Romain Gary, but Roman Kacew, and was of Jewish descent.

In *The Life Before Us* we meet the orphan boy Momo, whose real name is Mohammed. He does not know where he comes from, and he does not know how old he really is. The only thing he actually knows is that he is of Arab descent, because Madame Rosa, with whom he lives, insists that he needs a little Muslim upbringing. Madame Rosa has a past as a prostitute, and is herself Jewish — one of those who survived the Nazis’ extermination of the Jews during the war. Now she is getting old and frail, and we sense the beginning of a rapidly advancing dementia. She is no longer able to take proper care of herself, much less the children who have been placed with her by their prostitute mothers, who otherwise risk losing their children to the Welfare authorities. What might happen then is associated with horror and dread, without the children really quite grasping exactly what it is about.

Momo is the narrator and the “I” of the book. Madame Rosa claims that he is 10 years old, but later it turns out that he is 14 and that she has held back his age because she is afraid of losing him, her dearest child. The environment they are part of consists of prostitutes, transsexuals, and poor immigrants, mainly from African countries.

Momo looks at the world with his child’s eyes and his own unbeatable logic. Many of the observations he makes are so funny that I howled with laughter along the way. With statements such as “As long as there is life, there is no peace to be had” (page 18), “She puts on quite a lot of makeup, but it is no use playing hide-and-seek at her age” (page 20), “It is completely ridiculous nowadays, now that all that is dead and buried, but Jews are impossible to get rid of, especially when they have been exterminated, they keep coming back to it” (page 36), and “I remember I said it straight out to her, you have to slim down in order to eat less, but it is terribly hard for an old person who is alone in the world. She needed more of herself. When you are not surrounded by love, it turns into fat” (page 51) — well, you just have to surrender completely.

And I continue on **page 108**:

> “In Africa they stick together in tribes where old people are very much in demand because of everything they can do for you when they are dead. In France there are no tribes because of selfishness. Monsieur Walumba says that France has become completely de-tribed, and that is why there are armed gangs who stay faithfully together and try to accomplish something. Monsieur Walumba says that young people need a tribe, because otherwise they become like drops in the ocean, and that drives them completely crazy. Monsieur Walumba says that everything is getting so big these days that there is no point in even counting until you get to a thousand. That is why old people, who cannot join together in armed gangs in order to exist, disappear without leaving an address and live hidden away in dusty corners. No one knows about them, especially in attic rooms without elevators, when they cannot shout to say that there is someone there, because they do not have the strength for that. Monsieur Walumba says that large forces of manpower ought to be sent in from Africa to look for old people every morning at six o’clock and drive away the ones who are beginning to smell, because no one comes to check whether the old person is still alive, and it is only when someone says to the caretaker that there is a smell in the stairwell that everything is explained.”

Screamingly funny, while at the same time there is a certain sadness over it all, because what little Momo is describing is poverty and loneliness in all their horror ... One does not need much imagination to understand what he is really talking about. And it is precisely the alternation between the humorous and the serious that is this novel’s strength, while Momo’s unbeatable logic runs through the book like a red thread. He is so brainwashed into doing everything in his power to avoid the Welfare authorities that even on the day when he actually has the chance to get away from a Madame Rosa who is no longer at her best — even then he does not seize the opportunity ...

When I received a reading copy of the book from the publisher, an article about the author — written by Gabi Gleichmann — came along with it. Here Gleichmann writes the following:

> “A world of drug abuse, racism, prostitution, misery, and segregation is described with immense insight. Thirty-five years after the book’s publication, its picture of life at the bottom of French society is more relevant than ever.

> The novel enjoyed enormous success. It is in fact the best-selling and most widely read book in the history of France. When it was crowned with the country’s highest literary distinction, the Goncourt Prize, it triggered wild speculation about who was hiding behind the name Emile Ajar. No one doubted that it had to be an important writer. Many great names were suggested. Gary too. But the critics dismissed this possibility with the argument: ‘Oh no, Gary does not have sufficient talent.’”

*The Life Before Us* is a fantastic novel in every way! The narrative style and the voice of the young boy Momo, who turns out to be somewhat older than Madame Rosa has told him, are carried through to the very tips of the fingers. The depiction of an environment consisting of people at the very bottom of the social ladder is solid and authentic, and here a solidarity is portrayed so strong that no one allows anyone to sink all the way to the bottom without reaching out a helping hand. It is precisely this solidarity that is described so touchingly that tears pressed on a few times. If it had not been for the fact that Agora Publishing’s edition of the book is so beautiful, with a solid binding one does not often see these days, I would have taken out my yellow highlighter and underlined the most wonderful passages in the book while reading it. But that was exactly what I did not feel like doing in this splendid copy of a book.

This is a book I am going to read several times before I die. And since I am on that subject, I must say that I wonder why the book has not been included in *1001 Books You Must Read Before You Die*. It would certainly have deserved a place there! Otherwise, I am very pleased that this book is now available to new readers! May more people open their eyes to this treasure of a book!

text:
One often has different angles of approach to a book. Mine was strong curiosity. Because why would my youngest daughter ask me—who have over 4,000 books in my library—whether I had read this one? And: she had just returned home from a year’s trip in Australia as a backpacker. So I ordered it. And I became even more curious because I received a copy published by Bazaar, because the book had its 20-year anniversary. And in his foreword—to this “special” edition—he says that he was sitting on Copacabana with blank pages in front of him, about to begin his—always difficult—book number 2. He is sitting there and sees a fisherman pulling up his anchors, and it strikes him: Santiago! We who have read Hemingway’s “The Old Man and the Sea” (which Coelho has also done) know that the old fisherman was called Santiago. And with that he has a beginning: He writes: The boy’s name was Santiago. And then he was underway.

Now I do not know whether he is already conscious here of the mysticism in a name. After reading the book, I would think so. How many cities there are called Santiago I do not know. Perhaps the best known is the capital of Chile. But in Spanish-speaking names (especially) it is a much-used male name. It comes from Jacob, of whom there are two who are known in the Bible; the first is in the Old Testament, and the second is St. James—Jesus’s brother, whom I believe pilgrims (people who travel with a GOAL in mind) use as their “logo.” (?)

And then there is this business of Maktub, which he places great emphasis on. Why? He himself says it can be translated as “It is written,” but you have to be born an Arab to understand it. Well, I asked someone who was born an Arab, and quite right; it was not only that which has already been written (as history), but that which was always meant to happen to us! (I do not know, I am not Arab, but only someone who opens a new book (for me) to read. And what do I read? Yes, a legend, but one made so cleverly by the author that much of it almost becomes realism. Magical realism, we might say. A writer’s technique that mixes reality with fantasy. Here it is done so well that both the factual and the extraordinary become something that can sound realistic. Put very strongly, by me.

Often one finds a partly strong social criticism that follows the story. And I find that Coelho does this masterfully in this book, as a book within the book. Santiago is a completely ordinary and down-to-earth shepherd. He sets out on a—in its starting-point’s realism—almost hopeless journey to reach a goal he does not even know how geographically far away is. But along the way he is also to, he is told, carry out his own story. (Or legend, if one wants. For he wants—like so many others of us—to find a treasure. In other words: become rich!

Mankind’s dream through all ages? (Perhaps that is why we play the lottery every week?) In any case:

Santiago meets many who want to convince him that his dreams, his journey, cannot be realized. We can begin with his father and the crystal merchant, perhaps first and foremost. Note that these are OLDER people who for one reason or another have let fear get the upper hand over their own dreams. In that sense Coelho is critical not only of those who have failed in their own lives, but even more of those who try to push their own bitterness onto those who actively want to strive to follow their dreams of reaching a goal.

Perhaps the clearest example of magical realism is in the concluding part of Part II, where Santiago is able to speak with the desert, the wind, and the sun; he persuades all these elements to help him prove to all the tribal chieftains that he is an alchemist.

In the end one can say that the magical realism is completed when a robber tells Santiago that his treasure is actually at the starting point of his journey: the shepherd’s hut in Spain. But Santiago is rewarded by the universe for his stubbornness and enthusiasm. The universe was on his side because of his own ability to learn patience, to believe in himself, to keep going and complete his journey, and because of how he masters the obstacles that arise along the way.

The book is well written. It becomes beautiful because love plays such a large role (as it does in all good books?) Here love is called Fátima. (A random name? Hardly. Muhammad’s eldest daughter was called Fátima.) Other things too have been placed into the book, done with some intention or other, I think! Without it mattering for reading the book, which, like all legends, fairy tales and the like, is pleasant reading and absolutely entertaining. But this old king. The King of Salem. Namely: Salem, which is believing Jews’ name for Jerusalem, or rather: Shalem, which means peace in Hebrew. And so on, and so on. Even the wind he calls the Levant is known in Asia and North Africa with the meaning “the land of the sunrise” (Egypt is one of these countries according to tradition), where the pyramids are.....

And these stones Urim and Thummim are, according to tradition, stones, or precious objects, which the high priest in ancient Israel used as tools for God’s WILL.

In any case: A book I will not forget. For several reasons. And none of them are religious!

I mentioned that the person who made me aware of the book—my youngest daughter—had just come home from a strenuous journey around the whole eastern Australian coast. She stayed overnight in so-called hostels. I note that the name of such hostels is often Maktub.

And: When you want something, the universe will always put itself on your side. (First said here in the book by the old King of Salem.)

This book overflows with what we can use as good quotations.

Honestly: Those who look at my favorite books or “follow me” may have noticed that I added “The Alchemist” and “The Old Man and the Sea” on the same day. For what is the case is this:

If I had not noticed that Coelho himself found this name by thinking of Hemingway, I might never have got around to reading this book.

My favorite quotation can just as well end my post: “WHAT HAPPENS ONCE WILL NEVER HAPPEN AGAIN. BUT WHAT HAPPENS TWICE WILL ALWAYS HAPPEN A THIRD TIME.”

For me this was a gem of a book, because it was so different from others I have read (and I have read many! = I am old), and it was well written, and one rarely gets so much adventure for adults. Here nothing has been spared: love (fortunately), wars (unfortunately), excitement, dangerous journeys, and everything ends well as it should.(?) And it is timeless.

Nothing is mentioned so that we have a peg to hang the course of events on in time-history. No year. No world war. etc. Good!!

I know it. I KNOW it! I cannot get around the prologue (for it does give us a peg in that respect: The events are closer to us in time than one might possibly think, if it were not for the prologue. For it shows us that what happens here is nevertheless placed in time: Oscar Wilde! That is, after this author wrote............:

For the alchemist picks up a book and quickly finds this author’s name. Oscar Wilde transformed a beautiful legend (about Narcissus) into an even more beautiful one. In other words, he “alchemized” as he turns a beautiful metal into an even more beautiful one: (gold).

.........the lake says: “I weep for Narcissus, but I never noticed that Narcissus was beautiful. I weep for Narcissus because each time he knelt beside my banks, I could see, in the depths of his eyes, the reflection of my own beauty.”

“What a beautiful story,” the alchemist said to himself.”

And I agree with that.
