text:
According to Bilden, there are three myths about food that shape the debate about the geopolitics of food here in Norway. The first is the local-food myth, which says that food produced nearby is more environmentally friendly than food that comes from far away. Bilden points out that if one includes the energy use in production, both Norwegian meat and Norwegian vegetables fall short compared with food produced at more southerly latitudes. The second myth is the resource myth. Bilden claims, rather surprisingly, that it is a myth that there is too little food in the world, and that the problem is due to distribution, not a shortage of food. The third myth concerns trade: according to Bilden, there are a number of actors in the debate about the geopolitics of food who claim that only market liberals believe that trade is better than aid.

Throughout the book, Bilden wants to launch a solidarity-based trade policy that confronts these myths. Bilden claims that the reason these myths have survived for so long is poor journalistic work and a lack of competence about global development trends in the Norwegian press. He also attacks both the Centre Party and the Trade Campaign, which, according to Bilden, advocate a protectionist policy that fails to acknowledge that development happens first and foremost through trade.

So what kind of Norwegian trade policy does Bilden want? First and foremost, he argues for a strong increase in Norwegian food imports from countries in the South, in step with a reduction in Norwegian food production. Bilden wants to do this by reducing production subsidies in Norwegian agriculture, and shifting the support over to the preservation of cultural landscapes and biological diversity. According to Bilden, this will both benefit the environment and promote development in the countries in the South that need the export income. Bilden also relies on the views of the African Union, which among other things argues that only countries in the South have the right to protect their own production against imports.

There are many good points and much that is good in Bilden’s book. Bilden’s visits to food people and farmers in the South and the North challenge anyone who is concerned with agriculture and trade to think through what the right medicine is in trade policy. He also paints a credible picture of Africa as a “horn of plenty,” where the chance of becoming overweight is every bit as threatening as hunger for surprisingly many people. What nevertheless weakens Bilden’s book is that in quite a few areas he simplifies the picture of the global food situation and the existing power constellations. This becomes a paradox when his stated purpose with the book is to kill off Norwegian myths about food and power.

The most startling simplification Bilden makes is when he claims that there is no food shortage in the world, and that there will not be one in the next 40 years either! Bilden has found this information on a website that is part of the UN Millennium Project and also in a report from the UN’s agricultural division, FAO, and he therefore accepts the information at face value. The problem is that the FAO report is based on a number of assumptions that each seem unrealistic. One example is that FAO, in its report, has not taken into account that much of the agricultural area will be used for energy production in the future. In addition, FAO assumes an 80% increase in agricultural yields in the countries of the South over the next 40 years, on the same area of land. This seems unrealistic both with regard to the energy use this will require, and with regard to the challenges many countries face in relation to climate change, for example erosion and drought. A number of international experts also reach conclusions diametrically opposed to Bilden’s. For example, the founder of the Worldwatch Institute, Lester Brown, has written that the record-high grain prices of recent years are the beginning of an era in which food shortages and the struggle over scarce resources will characterize the world.

Bilden is of course right that locally produced food is often far less environmentally friendly than imported food. One striking example is Norwegian tomatoes, which are often produced in energy-guzzling greenhouses. In that case it goes without saying that Spanish and Moroccan tomatoes grown in open fields are far more environmentally friendly. At the same time, as a reader one misses a broader discussion in Bilden of the crisis in industrial agriculture. With the global challenges we face linked to climate change and the use of energy, water and chemical pesticides, there is no doubt that industrial agriculture over the next few decades must become far more environmentally friendly and extensive. Whether we invest in food production in the North or the South, today’s industrial agriculture represents one of the greatest threats to the environment on earth.

In such a situation, is it particularly wise to invest less in Norwegian agriculture, which has better conditions for environmentally friendly operation than most other Western countries? We have great access to water, less need to use chemical pesticides because of low infection pressure, small farms and very large outfield resources. Norwegian agricultural policy has admittedly failed, and therefore we have today ended up with an energy-intensive and not very environmentally friendly agriculture. The conditions for the opposite are nevertheless the very best.

There is also reason to highlight Bilden’s vision for a more solidarity-based development policy as a simplified picture of the challenges countries in the South face. Even though Bilden spends a few pages at the end of the book discussing ideas about how the World Trade Organization can become more democratic, it is striking how much faith he has that a new trade agreement will give poor countries the chance to develop their way out of poverty through trade in food. Bilden claims that the WTO, because of the consensus principle—all countries must agree before anything is adopted—is a suitable organization for securing the interests of poor countries. The challenge is that all experience shows that the poor countries are run over in these negotiations, despite the consensus principle. For example, it is not difficult to agree with Bilden that Western countries’ export subsidies often destroy markets in the South, and that such subsidies ought to be illegal. Still, it seems unrealistic that these subsidies will be removed through the WTO negotiations. How, then, can we continue to have confidence in this system?

Food and trade policy is an extremely complex political field. Kaare Bilden deserves credit for making a wholehearted attempt to unite environmental and development concerns in his vision for a new trade policy. It is therefore a pity that he has to simplify the picture of the resource situation and the power constellations in the world community so much in order to make his vision seem credible.

text:
My generation’s view of the original inhabitants of America was shaped to a large extent by comics (my favorite was *Texas*) and films in the 1950s and 1960s. Later this perception was modified somewhat, fortunately.

In 1994 I bought the book *The Native Americans. An Illustrated History* on a reservation in New Mexico. It is edited by Betty Ballantine and Ian Ballantine and is a colossus of 480 huge pages, packed with the history of those who first came to the American continent. The aim of the book is “to help bridge, if not end, the communication gap of misunderstandings and false images that have so plagued Indian-white relations” (p. 20). How well the editors have succeeded is hard to say, but the effort is in any case beyond reproach!

In the introduction Alvin M. Josephy Jr. early on attacks the widespread Eurocentric view of the native inhabitants –

>an ingrained conviction on the part of those who first came to the Americas from Europe, as well as by their American descendants, that their cultures, values, religions, lifeways, abilities, and achievements were more advanced and of a higher order than those of the Indians. It followed, therefore, that they deemed the Indians to be inferior peoples–uncivilized Stone Age savages, perhaps even subhuman–and their cultures irrelevant or barbaric and dangerous to civilized mankind.

(p. 16). When the Spanish and Portuguese conquerors came to the continent, he says, there were fifty million native inhabitants there; a few centuries later the number had been reduced to 250,000. And he shows how their culture and values have systematically been destroyed as a result of the idea that they were inferior and of lesser worth.

The account begins with the first immigrants coming from Asia to America, those who gradually “developed sophisticated forms of art, elaborate political and social structures, intricate intellectual patterns, mathematics, handicrafts, agriculture, writing, complex religious and belief systems, imaginative architecture” (p. 25). Yes, it is probably right when it says “Native American architecture matched anything Columbus had seen in his travels” (p. 26). It continues with various aspects of history and culture and shows, among other things, that textbooks up to the time of publication had been wrong in saying that there were only three areas in what corresponds to present-day USA where the inhabitants practiced agriculture. The last was in the Northeast. Gradually life on the prairie and in the forests is presented, together with, among other things, religion and language, the story of Pocahontas, handicrafts, agriculture, hunting, the use of the horse (the horse originally came from America, migrated to Asia and then came back with the Europeans), the tragic encounter with alcohol, participation in the Civil War, life on the reservations (President Grant wanted to use the reservations to make the “Indians” into “whites”), Geronimo, the massacre at Wounded Knee and the work to become full citizens.

Then the Indigenous population enters the twentieth century – “Against all odds” (p. 383). We get to see how representatives took part in working life in the larger society, such as when they helped build bridges in New York City, as I can remember an emigrated uncle telling me early in the 1960s. An ironworker from the Mohawk tribe put it like this, by the way (p. 389):

>A good ironworker is afraid of high places. I don’t want to work with no fool who’s not a little bit afraid of being up so high. It’s the fear that gives you the edge, that keeps you alert. … No, a Mohawk is afraid of heights just like the next guy. The difference is, the Mohawk is willing to deal with it.

The last part is about the complicated conditions in the twentieth century, including participation in the Second World War, how the federal government bought up the land, and how the struggle continued.

The account is thus largely limited to today’s USA and a little about Canada, and we follow the Spanish conquest of this part of the continent, with a thorough treatment of de Soto’s expedition and the attempts at rebellion against the conquerors. For me it is especially interesting to read about how the Spaniards destroyed the village of Acoma in present-day New Mexico (the illustration is “Acoma Pueblo” by Lloyd Townsend; I have visited the town, which plays a role in the background story of Lesli M. Silko’s short story “Tony’s Story” (fiction could have been treated more thoroughly in the book, by the way). Later, rebellion against the new republic and war against the settlers are dealt with, all the time with relevant quotations in the margins and large and small illustrations. One of the marginal texts deals with “California Genocide”:

>Of all Indian regions in America, California, with its medley of different native groups peopling diverse ecoregions, suffered the most after the United States won the these lands from Mexico. In village after village, rampant brutality became commonplace as gold miners, ranchers, and townsfolk swarmed into river valleys throughout the northern half of the state.
>It was not uncommon for the government to effectively reward the ‘volunteer armies’ who cleared out unprotected Indian villages. In one year, 1851–52, California authorized over one million dollars to reimburse vouchers submitted by loosely organized miners and new settlers for expenses incurred during their terrorizing raids. The Sinkyone Indians were one group stunned by these assaults.
>Before the gold rush there were over four thousand in the Humboldt County villages; then, as one victim from Needle Rock later remembered, they were ruthlessly set upon, ‘About ten o’clock in the morning, some white men came. They killed my grandfather and my mother and my father. I saw them do it. I was a big girl at that time. Then they killed my baby sister and cut her heart out and threw it in the brush where I ran and hid. …. I didn’t know what to do. I was so scared that I guess I just hid there a long time with my little sister’s heart in my hands.’ At the close of the 1860s all that was left of the Sinkyone was a handful of survivors with ghastly memories of what had happened.
>In the period between 1855 and 1870, such brutality was the rule rather than the exception. By 1865 the Wintu, for instance, numbering over fourteen thousand a quarter century earlier, were reduced to fewer than one thousand weakened, who disoriented survivors. The story was repeated throughout the foothills, as community after community experienced the same nightmare.

“Our culture is high and rich!” says Jens Bjørneboe (yes indeed, massacres of Europeans are also mentioned, as in the chapter where John Vanderlyn’s “The Death of Jane McCrea” is one of the illustrations: anger shines from the eyes of the two who are about to execute and scalp a white woman …).

The book is illustrated with photographs and copies of paintings, engravings and drawings, such as “Arrival of Hendrick Hudson in the Bay of New York, September 12, 1609” by Frederic A. Chapman from 1868 (a good example of an interpretation of what must surely have been the mood when the native inhabitants discovered the Europeans), “Discovery of the Hudson River” by Alfred Bierstadt (1874), “Buffalo Hunt” by George Catlin and Frank C. McCarthy’s “The Buffalo Runners.” The strongest impression is perhaps made by “The Trail of Tears” by Robert Lindneux, which shows the deportation of the Cherokee people. Alfred Jacob Miller’s “The Trapper’s Bride” (1850) shows that relations between Europeans and native inhabitants could be many-sided …

I do not have enough background knowledge to go into the sources and check how the authors have used them. But all in all, the book testifies to thorough work to document their own identity and human dignity. “There is,” a native inhabitant has said, “no ‘better’ or ‘worse’, only different. That difference has to be respected whether it’s skin color, way of life, or ideas.” (p. 21).

# An Adventurer’s Philosophy of Life

In an [article](http://www.dagbladet.no/nyheter/1999/01/11/153096.html) by Hege Duckert in Dagbladet on 11.01.1999, she begins with the following words: “It is a paradox that Arne Næss, one of Norway’s most prominent thinkers, is most famous for using his legs” ... “legendary for his climbing expeditions.” Because that is what he is best known for! That he is also a philosopher is something most people who have a university education behind them know. For who does not remember struggling through *The History of Philosophy* volumes I and II in order to take examen philosophicum? I still have the books standing on my shelves, almost 30 years later ... Full of underlinings, markings, etc.

Arne Næss was born in 1912 and died in 2009, almost a hundred years old. During his life he managed to give logic and philosophy a key position in the academic and intellectual life of Norway in the post-war period, to quote [Wikipedia](http://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Næss). He wrote quantities of books and articles on various themes within philosophy and logic, and the mere fact that his textbooks were part of the syllabus for the university’s preliminary exam for a number of years has, as mentioned, meant that everyone with a degree behind them has some relationship to the philosopher.

To be completely honest, it is not often that I read philosophical works at all. But when I came across this small and relatively modest book at a book sale some years ago, I thought that maybe it was time for a little philosophical updating. Even so, it took a few years before I finally got it read — yes, not until I found the book as an audiobook at the library and thought that “now I shall get started!” It also fit well into my little project of reading literature with a focus on [happiness](http://rosemariechr.blogspot.com/search/label/lykke), increased quality of life, and so on.

For an untrained “philosopher,” it is not easy to briefly reproduce what Arne Næss’s book is about. He embraces so many themes along the way, and having to summarize in a few sentences what the essence of his philosophy of life is, is difficult. One common denominator, however, is the importance of enthusiasm! How much more fun is it not to learn something difficult if the teacher or master is enthusiastic about what he or she is doing? As opposed to sitting and listening to a dry and boring lecturer ... Besides, we should stop being so concerned with “the right” answers, and rather concentrate on asking questions, being more wondering instead of concluding. In Næss’s thinking, moreover, feelings and reason are something that belong together — not opposites, as we are traditionally trained to think. He makes a case for bringing feelings in as part of research.

I found the part of the book that dealt with emotional maturation the most interesting of all. Næss asks, for example, what it was that made young Norwegians allow themselves to be recruited by the Nazis during the Second World War, and carry out the most grotesque acts of torture during interrogations of their countrymen. Why was it, to only a small degree, men — because it was mostly men it was about — over 30–40 years old who took part in such acts? Næss analyzes the problem and concludes that the explanation most likely is the lack of emotional maturation in people between 15 and 25 years old. Emotionally mature people, namely, were not so easily dazzled by the rhetoric of Nazism.

One of the chapters in the book is called “One Should Only Learn What One Feels Like Learning.” In the introduction he writes:

> “In an affluent society like Norway, we need both a pedagogy and an educational system that take feelings into account. We talk about education. I believe we should also talk about inner formation: inner values such as wonder, creativity, and imagination. There are many subjects that are excellently suited to promoting such qualities, but then we must educate teachers who are allowed to be personal and shape their teaching plans more freely. In addition, the knowledge requirements must be lowered — to learn well is to learn slowly. Learning only becomes effective if the pupils and students are occasionally allowed to concentrate on something they burn for.” (page 143)

Otherwise, it is — Næss claims — a paradox that other languages do not have a word that covers our Norwegian concept of “utdannelse” (“education”). “Dannelse” (“formation” or “cultivation”), on the other hand, is a concept that carries great weight in other countries too. Næss also believes that when one talks about the learning of new skills and knowledge, one should in addition be conscious of the unlearning that necessarily also takes place.

It is probably no coincidence that the book’s last chapter is called “The Art of Living — Doing Small Things in a Big Way,” because here Næss summarizes what significance there is in enjoying the life one lives.

> “Many older people have a strong ability to handle problems on the spot and to see what is most important in existence. Many young and middle-aged people realize this too late because they do not take the time to seriously question their priorities. The decisive thing is not exactly what one spends one’s time on. The most important thing is how one engages oneself, and what strength one puts into it. The art of living is being able to do small things in a big way. I want to launch a ‘well-being formula’ that shows how life can always turn out to be acceptable, despite all pain, as long as we burn for what we do.” (page 163)

In a way I think Arne Næss’s book sums up much of the same that I have seen in other literature dealing with themes such as the art of living, happiness, and the like. In order to achieve the good life, one must prioritize things that engage one, that inspire enthusiasm and make one glow with interest. If “everything” just becomes a duty-run, the joy of living is killed. In our society, where we actually have everything and where the possibilities are so many that we almost have to consult experts in order to be able to make even the simplest choices in rather too many contexts, it is appropriate to remind ourselves of the importance of following our feelings, even if these cannot always be explained rationally. The chance that the choice will be right for us is great when we follow our feelings. This is at least the essence I have drawn from this book, which I found very interesting, even though the material was at times a little difficult to access.

The book is well suited to creating reflection on important themes in life, and Næss is very concerned with emphasizing that there is no ready-made philosophy of life that can be formulated once and for all. A philosophy of life becomes — like most other things in this life — as one lives, and is constantly changing. What is important to one person does not have to be so for another. In any case, we must move away from the idea that being so critical of everything and everyone is considered so much more intellectual than being open and having the ability to let oneself be inspired!

It was actually especially fun to listen to the audiobook version, since the aging philosopher himself read the introductions to the chapters in the book. Erik Hivju, for his part, functioned excellently as narrator.

This gets **dice roll five**.

# A very successful new book in the Jarle Klepp series!

In this fifth book in the Jarle Klepp series, Jarle has managed to become 38 years old. He is happily married to his Iselin, with whom he has had two children: Åshild, who is six, and Sven, who is not quite three. That he would end up as a teacher like his father was perhaps not quite what he had dreamed of, but basically he is happy with that too. Because as long as he gets to read the books he wants, listen to the music he loves, follow some of the series that are on TV, have good moments together with his wife and not least with his children - yes, then he is a happy man. He must be able to say that!

From the earlier books about Jarle Klepp, we know about his upbringing with an alcoholic father. It all ended with his mother divorcing him, because she could no longer stand the wretched life with a man whose greatest interest in life was to drink, drink, drink ... A man who criticized her because she did not drink together with him. Did they perhaps no longer have anything in common? She who was only boring and mean. After the divorce, things quickly went downhill for the father, who - even though he died of a heart attack - actually drank himself to death, now that he no longer had anyone he needed to pull himself together for.

Jarle has long since deeply distanced himself from his father and everything he stood for. It is many years since his father died, and Jarle has all along thought - to the extent that he has thought - that this thing with his father is a closed chapter in his life. Until New Year’s Eve in 2010, when he is going out to buy sparklers for his children and suddenly finds himself facing a girl from the past ... A girl who was the daughter of one of his parents’ friends, where his father eventually went every single weekend to drink, since it was so lousy at home. A girl who knows the family’s deepest secrets, secrets Jarle would prefer to forget. But not only that - this girl even knows more about his father than he himself does. Does he really want to know about this? Is it not enough, what he already knows about his father? Does he need to know what really happened when he, his father, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend went hiking on Hardangervidda one summer in his childhood? That time when a harrowing quarrel ended with his brother and his girlfriend leaving them - a drunk father and a frightened eleven-year-old - in the middle of Hardangervidda? And does he need to know what experiences this girl herself has had in relation to his father?

In any case - the past comes crashing in on Jarle, a man who has avoided at any cost digging down into his own darkness, for fear of what he might find there. At the same time he struggles to find his own way of being a father, and now and then he has to painfully acknowledge that he is in fact his father’s son no matter how much he dislikes thinking about this. Even if he does not have alcohol problems and is far more loving than his own father was ... What does he do when his precocious little six-year-old begins talking about how she misses her grandfather, a man she has never met - yes, precisely because of that!, and demands that Jarle take her to his grave and tell her what he was like ... ?

I think this is a book one either loves or feels rather indifferent toward. I myself am among those who believe that this is the best Jarle Klepp book Tore Renberg has written! At the beginning I thought that it cannot possibly be possible to write so intensely and vividly about this without having experienced it firsthand! And perhaps this book has more autobiographical traits than we readers realize. But why some people absolutely have to draw parallels to Knausgård (a writer I otherwise love!) and then almost describe this book as a cornucopia, I have no understanding of. For my part I think “So what!” It would be naive to believe that writers do not make use of their own experiences when they write literature. Perhaps it is as simple as there actually being something universal about growing up with a parent who is more preoccupied with intoxication than with the family’s welfare? At the same time, I think that I as a reader must accept that this book actually is about Jarle Klepp and not about the author!

This book really got under my skin! At the same time as Renberg writes about Jarle’s sad childhood with a father who drank, the book is full of touching sequences about him and his relationship with his children. About little Sven, who is in the process of leaving the baby stage and becoming a boy, about the daughter Åshild, who constantly challenges her father with her explosive self ... a girl who is a true version of today’s young negotiating generation, and who, despite her young age, is not willing to take no for an answer, at least not before she understands why. And about Jarle’s joy when he discovers that the children know how to appreciate his own taste in music ...

While I was reading the book, it happened that I played the songs that were mentioned on an iPad with YouTube access, which I had within reach. It added an incredible amount of life to the text, to put it that way. The only thing I basically missed finding out something about was Lotte - Jarle’s daughter from a one-night stand in his youth - and her place in his life. Otherwise, I want to add that the way Renberg writes in this book is quite different from in the other Jarle Klepp books. Perhaps it has something to do with his being closer to Jarle this time? Renberg writes well and has numerous sharp observations along the way, which hit me in the heart and made me think, “yes, that is exactly how it is!” All in all, a very successful book, which I think deserves **a die roll of six**! And I say: yes please, I would gladly have more books about Jarle Klepp!

Here is a link to my blog post about the book: [Tore Renberg: “These Are My Old Days”](http://rosemariechr.blogspot.com/2011/10/tore-renberg-dette-er-mine-gamle-dager.html)

# 1960s Tristesse

In “I’m Going to Make You So Happy” we are introduced to eight families who live in one stairwell of an apartment block in Trondheim in the mid-1960s. Outwardly fairly similar, but highly different once we get to know them, as it turns out. While the men are at work, a teeming life goes on among the stay-at-home wives in the block.

Sound carries so much, so very much, between the flats that it is barely possible to have a private life. This bothers the women, who want to have something to themselves. Everyone keeps watch on everyone else, and is hungry for news in a time when, basically, nothing ever happens. We get a tiny glimpse into the men’s world, but most of all this is about the women; the first generation of women who had moved far away from their home places, and who had to create something entirely their own from scratch, almost without role models. Who are in the phase of establishing themselves, and who fill their weekdays with children, cleaning, gossiping and weekly magazines ...

At a time when the housewife role was associated with both pride and honor, and when everything was supposed to be spotlessly clean, preferably gleaming, and when all food was made from scratch to save a few øre here and a few øre there—in order to stretch the tight household budgets as far as possible—no one talked about the oppression of women. If anything, it had to be the women themselves who oppressed one another, as they gossiped about anyone and everyone who was the slightest bit different from themselves. Well, if it was to be acceptable to be different, one had to be different in the right way. But pity the person who did not iron all her clothes, who did not take the stair cleaning seriously enough, who did not make food from scratch—then she really got it!

One married couple in the block has just had a little baby, but everything is not as it should be. The baby no longer cries, the mother is clearly in a postnatal depression, and she and her husband communicate extremely badly. Another married couple is not quite like the others, because the husband is a translator and in that sense has a free profession where he can come and go as he pleases, while the wife, who is English, runs a hairdressing salon in the kitchen to supplement their income. At the top of the block towers the Foss family; he a travelling salesman in Toro soup packets, she a tasty morsel of a woman who is slim, always tanned and with red-painted nails, but who is bored to death while her husband is away travelling, since they have not yet had children for her to fill her days with. The way to a highball glass or two to make the long days more bearable is not far ...

And then we have little Nina, Karlsen’s motherless daughter, who does not have her own key to the flat and always wanders around almost like a homeless person, smelling of pee from her dirty clothes because her father never manages these housewife things, and does not have all the understanding in the world for a small child’s needs either. But little Nina has talents in mathematics that are completely unique. We sense a neglected dandelion child, who will probably manage, but who on the way up to adulthood will have a winding road, as she yearns for a love her father is not capable of giving her, and who therefore thinks it is okay to sit on the caretaker’s lap, even though he shakes so strangely and whispers “my girl” into her hair. In addition, we have the housewives who manage everything perfectly, and who use themselves as the measuring stick when they pass their strict, strict judgments on the others, who in their view clearly do not measure up.

The book is divided into three. In the first part we get to know all the families. In the second part we follow a door-to-door salesman from door to door in the stairwell. He sells peepholes. For nineteen kroner each family can have a peephole with wide-angle glass installed, so that they can see who is ringing the bell, and thus can choose not to open the door to just anyone. On his way up the floors, we get his interpretation of what he sees inside each of the flats. In the final part, it is the housing cooperative’s growing rat problems that must be dealt with.

I think one has to have lived a while to get the full benefit of this book, because its strength clearly lies in the easily recognizable elements from this period of history. Otherwise I think one may well experience this book as a little boring, with the housewives mostly preoccupied with cleaning, cleaning and still more cleaning. But that was how it was! And Anne B. Ragde has really done thorough research in order to write this book! Many times I found myself sitting and roaring with laughter at the funny character descriptions. Like the woman who seriously considers having another child when her husband starts talking about closing down his office to save money, and sitting at home with his translations. She does not want him at home! She wants to have her days entirely at her own disposal! Or the woman who recoils when her husband suggests that she should get a job. Has she not just got married precisely to avoid having to work outside the home, perhaps?

The fixation on “magazine day” as a high point of the week I remember well myself. Even the dreadful sunlamp is included in the book! The ladies who chose to keep themselves outside the close-knit gossip environment among the women really got it. Did they perhaps think they were better than the others? As they walked around with their noses in the air and would not stoop to mixing with them ... And if, on top of everything, one was childless, one was met with violent skepticism. Was one even feminine when it came down to it? In a time when there was a shortage of most things, it attracted great attention if someone got a freezer or had a telephone installed. Making a long-distance call was horribly expensive, and one did not do that at all hours.

I think Anne B. Ragde has succeeded well in her project of writing about the housewives of the 1960s! With her customary humor and warmth she portrays the housewives’ simple lives in an optimistic age, where most things pointed upward. With the Cuban Missile Crisis as a backdrop in a time when the position of the radio was central in every home, and when television was not yet common, she confidently hits the style of an epoch about which loads of books have been written, but never in the way she does it here. Even though it is natural to draw a certain parallel to the Norwegian film “Støv på hjernen,” this book is about so much more. Here there is also more everyday realism. Furthermore, I would like to emphasize that the book comes across as linguistically well worked through. Whether it will remain as great literature in posterity is hard to say, but at any rate it rises well above the average mediocrity where most bestsellers are to be found. So here it is a **five on the dice**!

# A satirical sideways glance at social-democratic Norway in the years 1980–2010

When Frode Grytten comes out with a new book, this is always connected with great excitement! And he does not disappoint this time either. To read his sharp portrayals of people and environments, first and foremost far from the noise and bustle of the city and then, not surprisingly this time too, partly from Odda, is a delight! The village’s merciless and critical view of anything and anyone who is even a tiny bit different from everything else is anything but inclusive. If you do not fit in, it is over and out for you!

**“Saganatt”**, or the Lunde trilogy as it is called, is divided into three parts, and in reality contains three fairly independent novels. As in “Bikubesong,” however, there is a connection between the stories, as will become apparent after a while.

In the first part, **“Kom søndag,”** we are introduced to Arvid Lunde, who comes ashore in Odda in the late autumn of 1980. With his high-water trousers — or spring-tide trousers, as they are consistently referred to — he is immediately noticed, weighed and found wanting by those who look at him. Preferably by the boys from the smelting works, who frequent the pub “Smeltaren.”

Arvid Lunde has been offered a job as a teacher, and has left his former life in Bergen in order to start anew in Odda. For the first weeks he has to live at the place’s only guesthouse, where the receptionist Blondie works, a woman who always goes after newly arrived men in the hope that they will get her away from this dreary place. She tries her luck with Arvid too, and the fact that he rejects her makes her never speak to him again. Arvid is wildly enthusiastic about Odda, and he has a vision of taking an active part in the labour movement. But his commitment is not quite believed, because he is so different from the typical industrial worker. Nor does he fit in with the power elite in the village, and he therefore remains a fairly lonely man through most of the 1980s. There is a lot of speculation about him as a person. Is he perhaps gay, since he has no woman in his life? The gay rumours are eventually replaced by rumours that he is involved with a 17-year-old girl whom he has reluctantly agreed to give extra lessons at home in his bedsit. He truly becomes an outcast man, but he does not leave Odda for that reason.

The village’s hostility toward Arvid Lunde takes a new turn when it turns out that he has gone and become rich almost “in secret” during the years he has lived in Odda. The people of the village do not like rich people, while at the same time they cannot help admiring him, a man who has achieved what they all in fact go around dreaming of: getting a lot of money fast! In time Arvid becomes a real yuppie, a successful financier, and moves to Oslo. He gets himself a woman too. Even a son. Until the financial crisis brings most of it to a brutal end ...

In part two — **“I morgon er det mondag”** — we meet the furniture dealer Harold Lunde, formerly a successful businessman who in his time took over the furniture shop after his father. Harold Lunde’s shop stood for quality, and the running of the business was based on the fact that he knew all his customers, knew who were good and bad payers. And it could have continued like that, had it not been for IKEA coming to Åsane in Bergen, and competing him completely out onto the sidelines with its shoddy furniture. That, in fact, he does not get over.

Furniture-Lunde has two sons — the previously mentioned Arvid Lunde, as well as Jan Lunde, who is a journalist and lives in Oslo. Neither of the sons likes him, and after the scandal around Arvid, Harold no longer speaks about him. His wife Marny has disappeared into the fog of dementia and barely remembers who he is. So there he stands — without a livelihood, long since bankrupt, with a wife who has forgotten him and with children and grandchildren who do not want contact with him. He carries out one last desperate act when he travels to Sweden to kidnap IKEA’s Ingvar Kamprad. He wants revenge!

In part three — **“Den åttande dagen”** — we find ourselves around Oslo in 2010. To the extent that this last part is connected with the two preceding ones, it is because we meet Robby Lunde, the son of Arvid Lunde, who has managed to get into his twenties. Gerhardsen and Bratteli drive around in Toyota Corollas to make sure that good social democrats live their lives in accordance with the party book. They are so-called “unliving,” and no one can see them. At regular intervals they prevent scandals in which elected representatives are involved from reaching the public’s ears. Whether it is the man who has cashed in the pension of his long-dead mother for more than thirty years, while the mother has been frozen in the freezer ... and many other cases which, if they came out, would have damaged social democracy and its spirit ...

Parts 1 and 2 of the book engaged me 110 percent. The story of Arvid Lunde and his brutal meeting with rural Norway is in many ways exactly the way I expect it to be when I am facing a Grytten book! Even though part 2 goes a little over the top toward the end, it was perhaps the part of the trilogy that touched me most of all. The story of Harold and Marny losing each other, because Marny’s dementia becomes more and more advanced, until Harold in the end can no longer keep her at home, is heartbreaking. And even more heartbreaking was reading about both spouses being stripped of authority in relation to each other when Marny finally ended up in a nursing home, and was almost not given permission to come home — not by Harold, but by the nursing home staff. In the last part I basically fell off the wagon quite a bit, I must admit. At the beginning I did not quite understand the aim and purpose of this part, and even though the pieces eventually fell somewhat more into place, I still struggled to fully understand the connection. I simply did not get very much out of this third part. It affects my assessment of the book, which should have been a six on the dice, but which instead “only” becomes a five. Otherwise I must add that it is especially part three that contains a load of humour and witty exchanges of lines, which made me roar with laughter many times. Grytten is and remains one of the greatest living Norwegian authors I know of!

I am convinced that this is a book I will take great pleasure in reading again in a few years.

The Hungarian Jew Andras Lévi has had a dream fulfilled that he had hardly dared to hope would come true: he has received a scholarship to the prestigious architecture school Ecole Speciale in Paris. In Hungary it is not easy for Jews to get an education, because the number of Jews admitted is very limited. When he packs the few belongings he owns into a suitcase and is about to leave for Paris in 1937, he is given a letter from some acquaintances of his parents, which he is to deliver to the mysterious C. Morgenstern. Little does he know then that this woman, who makes her living as a dance instructor, will eventually become the great love of his life.

After only a short time in Paris, the unthinkable happens; the scholarship is stopped for unknown reasons, and for a while things look very bleak for Andras. But then, fortunately, he gets a job as an errand boy at the Sarah Bernhard theatre, and it thus becomes possible for him both to pay his tuition fees and to survive in some way.

In the years before the outbreak of the Second World War, it is not entirely safe to be a Jew in Paris, because hatred of Jews runs deep among people, and there are many—not only the Nazis—who want to have the Jews removed from society. In the beginning it is above all far-right groups that quite literally beat up and even kill Jews. Gradually the Jews are blamed for most of what is wrong. Even before France was occupied by the Germans, laws were introduced that made it almost impossible for Jews without French citizenship to remain there.

In the meantime, Andras and Klara, which is Miss C. Morgenstern’s real name, have begun a relationship. Klara is almost ten years older than Andras, but he does not care about this in the slightest. He loves Klara and she is the one he wants. Klara, who is a Hungarian in exile and who is hiding a secret so dreadful that she will not reveal it to just anyone for the life of her ...

Eventually Andras is forced to leave France and return to Hungary. Klara goes with him because she does not want to leave the man who has, by then, become her husband. In Budapest, however, a rather unkind fate awaits. Even though Hungary was perhaps not the country that treated its Jews worst, not even after the country became allied with Germany, Jews in particular were called up to labour camps, where conditions were so miserable that it was more a matter of luck than anything else that some survived at all. Andras, like his male family members—including two brothers—and other Jews, is used, among other things, as a mine clearer along the border with the Soviet Union. Meanwhile Klara, who is pregnant with the couple’s first child, has to manage as best she can on her own. That is, she has her family around her, but she is unaware that her wealthy father is being pressured for large sums by Hungarian officials to ensure that her old secret is not brought up again.

The Second World War moves forward, and with this come suffering and death, hunger and frostbite ... Pure luck decides who survives. Most, however, are not so lucky ... We follow Andras’s and Klara’s families until the end of the war, which ends with Budapest being bombed to pieces. The few who managed to survive eventually fled to the United States ... In the meantime they had experienced their ally—Germany—occupying Hungary, which led to massive attacks on the Jewish part of the population. Around 400,000 Jews were killed in German concentration camps during the occupation. Their liberators, the Russians, ended up in the end as new occupiers, and the expected freedom therefore failed to arrive. The Battle of Budapest is, incidentally, considered one of the bloodiest battles of the Second World War, and it was the Russians who fought the Germans to gain control of the city. After long sieges of the city, the Germans finally gave up and capitulated in mid-February 1945. During the two-month occupation, the city’s Hungarians survived in what was left of the city, without access to new food supplies. By then 70% of the city had been bombed to pieces, and all the bridges that had once connected the districts of Buda and Pest were destroyed ...

This book of more than 700 pages was not so much as a single page too long! On the contrary, I felt that perhaps it went a little too quickly toward the end. Not since I read Hans Fallada’s “Every Man Dies Alone” last autumn have I been so thoroughly engaged by a book as when I read “The Invisible Bridge.” Some of this is of course because I am very fond of, and fascinated by, Hungary as a country, and some of it is because the Second World War, and especially the fate of the Jews, engages me strongly. While I was reading the book, I thought more and more about what had led Julie Orringer, a relatively young American author, to become so intensely interested in the fate of Hungarian Jews that she wrote this colossus of a novel. I got the answer when I read the afterword. For this is, not surprisingly, about her own family’s history, although the novel itself is fiction. At that point many pieces fell into place. I do not think it is possible to dig up so many details about what actually happened in Hungary without having other sources to go to than documents alone. Hungary shares the fate of all the other Soviet-occupied states that formerly made up the Eastern Bloc, where history was written to promote the Russification of the country and not to document the actual truth about what happened. Therefore I am left with a feeling of having read something quite unique, something about which not all that much has previously been written.

“The Invisible Bridge” is well written, deeply moving, interesting, brutal, and informative about Hungary’s role during the Second World War, seen from the standpoint of a couple of Jewish families. Orringer has conveyed the utterly surreal nature of the fate that befell the Jews without resorting either to clichés or tearjerker tendencies. Perhaps it was precisely the increasingly compressed narrative style toward the end that meant the most gruesome details did not come across as as tear-choked as they most likely otherwise could have become? Even though the book is very well written and even though the story is very interesting, I have been somewhat in doubt as to whether I should give it five or six on the dice. Among other things, I missed the truly good and deeply probing character portraits that books worthy of a six are marked by. When I nevertheless end up giving it **six on the dice**, it is the story and the uniqueness of its breadth and depth that have been decisive for me. The book is truly well worth reading, and I recommend it most warmly. I myself found the beginning of the book a little heavy, but after passing page 100, the pages practically turned themselves.

# On moral decline, cultural suicide and the Norwegian “integration tragedy,” etc.

I will not exactly deny that it was with a certain skepticism that I decided to read this book. The reason lies in some of the media statements that have come from the strongly media-focused historian of religion Hanne Nabintu Herland over the last few years. Quite a lot of her messages are so sharpened that they are more suited to provoking than to actually forming the basis for good and nuanced public debates. I do, however, understand very well that the media love to bring forward a commentator who is completely fearless and who can take the pressure when the storm is at its worst. And who does not shy away from giving the media what the media want — namely provocative and hard-hitting headlines in the news picture. And one must give her that — she is and remains an amusing breath of fresh air!

Herland believes that it is time to raise respect for Norwegian culture, and that there is no contradiction between holding on to one’s own cultural identity and living in ethnic diversity. Not least, she believes that the USA shows that this is possible. In interviews about the book, she has among other things stated that in “Alarm!” she makes a total reckoning with the culture-radical 68ers’ way of thinking. What she is referring to is the downgrading of one’s own ideals and values that has taken place for Europeans in general in the encounter with non-Western immigrants. She believes that today it is looked down upon if one highlights the great ideals and values that have made Europe a great civilization. The cultural suicide that we are in the process of committing in Europe, Herland believes, must stop. The fact that we are inclined to feel sorry for the immigrants who come here she characterizes as a form of racism.

So far, basically all well and good ... But at some point in the book, in my view, it tipped over so much that I had problems keeping up with the turns ... And I became so furious that I had to mobilize the strength to bother reading on. Some of what I reacted to most was outright personal attacks on named persons, and this after the author herself had criticized left-wing radicals for making personal attacks on named value-conservative people in society. In other words, she does precisely what she accuses others of doing. For example, I experienced the attack on the relationship expert Thue as ugly. I did not recognize the attitudes she attributed to him, and perceived her explanations as rather condescending.

Besides, it does not entirely seem as if Herland understands how laws are made in Norwegian society, that is, that these are passed by the Storting and not by whatever government is sitting at the time. One example of this is the church’s lack of follow-up of the Partnership Act, that is, some priests’ resistance to marrying homosexuals. Herland is horrified that politicians even try to force their values on the church in a secularized society, and believes that religion should be elevated above the secular. This is a line of reasoning I have no problem following when it comes to confessions of faith and/or church questions of a more theological nature. But that the church should be elevated above ordinary legislation that is meant to ensure that, for example, discrimination does not take place — there I drop off. Without interference from legislation, we would never have had female priests today, and everyone knows what a struggle it has been for homosexuals to be allowed to practice within this profession.

Furthermore, I think Herland goes rather far when she compares Norwegian society with the former Soviet Union, because she believes that people who think differently are punished so harshly. OK, I take the point — but at any rate, one does not kill people who think differently in a country like Norway, and one also does not risk a life sentence for having deviant opinions. If a public official, or someone who is on the public payroll, is not willing to follow the laws and regulations that apply to that person’s professional practice — well, then one must actually accept that a consequence may be that one loses one’s job ... without Norway thereby being characterized almost as a totalitarian society! I am almost inclined to state that it really is not possible to claim such a thing!

That neither Norway nor other countries in Europe have succeeded very well in integrating quite a few of the non-Western immigrants is, moreover, not difficult to agree with. Herland also has a point when she emphasizes that there have been some costs when we have privatized religion, because we have lost important society-building values along the way. One would think that European society was particularly suited to increasing people’s quality of life, because we have never had greater freedom, more material prosperity and more choices, but in fact it is to a large extent the opposite that has happened. It is enough to mention the number of suicides, especially among young men, drug abuse and loneliness among very many people.

Unlike Herland, however, I am optimistic about the future in a multicultural Norway. Perhaps another generational shift or two is needed before we are completely at the goal, but the way the very young socialize in a multicultural society is truly an example to follow! That in the meantime we must quota immigrants into working life is one of several measures that are needed, and this is not about feeling sorry for dark-skinned people. It is instead about breaking down existing prejudices among Norwegians through legislation! Just think how outrageous the business community found the requirement of 40% female participation on boards and councils! Do we really believe that there is not a sufficient number of competent women in Norwegian society? In a transitional phase one tried voluntariness, but then, unfortunately, sadly little happened. Legal regulation is actually necessary to reach such goals — and this is no different for immigrants, who experience that despite higher education they do not even get interviews.

Otherwise, I think Herland ought to limit herself to being a national pundit on what she undoubtedly knows a lot about, namely the history of religion, and be somewhat more cautious about coming up with too categorical opinions on socio-economic matters. Some of the claims about Norway’s oil money and the use of it are actually directly wrong. This disfigures an otherwise provocative book that is absolutely a fresh contribution to the public debate, where she obviously dares to put into words a number of conditions it is not entirely acceptable to speak loudly about. I do not entirely care for her style or the way she does this. And perhaps some of my antipathy is due to the fact that we have such totally different political standpoints. On the other hand, more voices are needed in the debate, and I respect the fact that she does not have the same opinions as I do! Finally, an important clarification: Herland is not a researcher, even if the media are fond of calling her that.

The remote classroom is a concept that has been developing since the 1980s. This term is attributed to Roxanne Hiltz, who defines it as “the use of computer-mediated communications to create an electronic environment similar to the forms of communication that normally occur in the conventional classroom.”

Through this environment, the student can access and carry out a series of actions that are typical of an in-person teaching process, such as talking, reading documents, doing exercises, asking the teacher questions, working in teams, etc. All of this takes place in a simulated way, without physical interaction between teachers and students.

Websites are used by each class to make educational material available to students and to enrich it with resources published on the Internet. Course programs, schedules, and information related to the course are also published in this space, and communication beyond the limits of face-to-face meetings is promoted between students and the teacher, or among students. This system allows students to become familiar with the use of Information Technologies. It also gives access to the materials for each class from any computer connected to the network, making it possible to keep the class updated with the latest publications from good sources—teachers—and especially in the case of large classes, students are able to communicate even outside class hours without having to attend consultation classes. They can share points of view with classmates and carry out group work. It also allows students to decide whether they are going to save the readings and class contents on a physical medium in order to read them from the computer screen, or whether they are going to print them.

This use of the virtual classroom as a complement to the in-person class has in some cases been the first step toward the distance modality, since the class is available in electronic format and on the Web, and this format is easier to adapt to the materials offered in semi-in-person or remote classes.

In the case of distance education, the virtual classroom takes on a central role, since it will be the space where the learning process is concentrated. Beyond the way in which distance education is organized, whether it is semi-in-person or remote, synchronous or asynchronous, the virtual classroom will be the medium of exchange where the class will take place. It is important that, in the design or choice of a system or type of virtual classroom, it be clear what students are expected to achieve in their distance learning and what elements this tool should contain in order to allow the learning experience to be productive.

Objectives This learning project offers an overview that will familiarize the learner with the subject of study in such a way that he or she identifies and defines its basic concepts; recognizes the most important authors and moments in the development of the discipline; can establish and classify the relevant topics of corporate image and its relationship with other fields; distinguishes the methodologies proper to its study, so that finally he or she may estimate the importance of the contribution of corporate image in broadening the understanding of organizations today.

Corporate image has to do with the perception that the publics have of an organization. Paul Capriotti, author of Corporate Branding, describes it as the set of “attributes that the publics associate with a company.” The corporate image sector is therefore in charge of managing these attributes of the identity of organizations and how they are communicated to the publics. It is through the correct management of the image that the organization becomes known to the publics, or in Capriotti’s words, “through corporate image the organization exists for the publics.”

When we speak about corporate image, it is necessary to explain in detail that corporate image has various attributes, which give value to the corporate image of an organization. It is important to determine the attributes on which a public builds the corporate image. Each public values different attributes in an organization. The attributes of corporate image are divided into current attributes and latent attributes, and the current attributes in turn are divided into main attributes and secondary attributes. The main attributes are those that a public expects to see in an organization, while the secondary attributes are those that the organization offers to its public but that are not specifically expected by the public. The main attributes are classified into basic attributes and discriminatory attributes. The basic attributes are those that describe what a public expects from an organization, that is, these attributes describe the “minimum basic requirement” demanded by the public. Meanwhile, the discriminatory attributes are those that the organization uses in order to differentiate itself from another organization. In conclusion, current attributes are those that at this moment make up the corporate image of an organization, while latent attributes are those that at this moment are not forming the corporate image of an organization, but that in the future may do so.

text:
Human beings interact with the world through bodily operations and mental processes. Mental processes include the processing of the information provided by the senses, the storage of information, reasoning, decision-making in order to react appropriately to events in the environment, and problem solving. Modern cognitive psychology is responsible for studying these processes, but unlike its nineteenth-century predecessor, it is not based on introspection. Modern cognitive psychology studies human behaviors, interpreted in terms of these processes, and together with cognitive neuroscience seeks to explain the processes in terms of the physiological functioning of the brain.

Mental or cognitive processes are very complex and interactive. There are no specific points at which one can say that one ends and another begins. However, for teaching purposes it is possible to group them into four different areas based on the process they carry out on the information that people receive from the environment. The processes related to the capture of information (sensation, perception, and attention) receive information from the environment and make it available to the other processes. The processes related to reaction (emotion and motivation) take the information and lead people to take actions. Memory is the process related to the storage of information, and the processes related to its processing (learning, thought, language, and intelligence) allow us to analyze both stored information and new information captured by the senses in order to adapt and modify the environment.

Sensation is the process that includes the capture of information by the senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, pain, pressure, temperature, proprioception, etc.) and its transmission to the brain. It is concerned with the mechanisms through which the receptor organs (eyes, ears, etc.) receive stimuli and encode them in order to transmit them to the brain through afferent neurons, especially with the minimum magnitude that a stimulus must have so that it can be reliably distinguished from its absence, known as the absolute threshold, and with the minimum difference that must exist between two stimuli so that the senses identify a difference, known as the minimum perceptible difference (MPD). It also makes use of signal detection theory to understand the processes that make it possible to differentiate a stimulus from the rest of the information in the environment, called noise, because that process sometimes fails (we see something that does not exist, we hear a sound that has not been produced, etc.) and what the implications of those errors are.

Psychology is the science that studies the mind and behavior in interaction with context. Although these concepts may sound familiar, they are notably difficult to define. Philosophers and scientists have tried for hundreds of years to delimit the entities we refer to when we use them, without reaching a definitive agreement. For that reason, one of the most obvious and natural questions when we become interested in this science is also one of the most difficult to answer: “What does psychology study?” In this learning project we will try to answer that question. We will not do so by proposing a definition, but by taking a high-level tour through this field of study. text:
It is the current opposed to psychoanalysis. Behaviorism maintains that psychology is the study of individual behavior in interaction with the environment. The influence of the environment is decisive in human and animal behavior. Psychology must focus on the study of what is observable: behavior.

Although remote antecedents can be found, the starting point of behaviorism is identified with two schools: the Russian and the American. Pavlov (1849-1936) is the main exponent of classical conditioning. In the United States, Thorndike’s connectionism (1874-1949), so important in psychopedagogy because of various contributions, and Watson’s behaviorism (1878-1858) stand out.

Behaviorism is one of the theories of learning that has lasted for the most years and has the greatest tradition. Although it does not fit completely into the new educational paradigms because it conceives learning as something mechanical, dehumanized, and reductionist, the reality is that many current programs are based on behaviorist proposals, such as breaking information down into units, designing activities that require a response, and planning reinforcement.

Behaviorism is a current of psychology inaugurated by John B. Watson (1878-1958) that defends the use of strictly experimental procedures to study observable behavior and denies any possibility of using subjective methods such as introspection.

Its theoretical foundation is based on the idea that a stimulus is followed by a response, this response being the result of the interaction between the organism that receives the stimulus and the environment. External observation is the only possible basis for the constitution of a scientific psychology.

This approach was greatly influenced by the pioneering research of the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov on animal conditioning, considering that the acts of life were nothing more than reflexes. From his observations with animals, he designed the scheme of classical conditioning.

According to Thorndike, learning was made up of a series of connections between a stimulus and a response, which were strengthened each time they generated a satisfactory state of affairs for the organism (law of effect). This theory provided the bases on which Skinner later built his entire structure regarding operant conditioning.

Reinforcement theory consists of describing the process by which the continued association of a certain response to a certain stimulus is increased when the subject obtains a prize or reward (positive reinforcement). Operant conditioning, developed from Skinner’s contributions, is the application of reinforcement theory. By using these principles in a positive way to stimulate optimized behavior in learning. If it is applied from its negative aspects, that is, when punishment is applied as negative reinforcement to extinguish or decrease the frequency of a response, the results are unclear because emotional reactive behaviors are produced, which disturb learning and invalidate the person.

This learning resource is a lesson originally created as teaching material for the learning project Direction and Management of Projects and Information Systems. One of the fundamental aspects of project management is organizing the work team that will carry it forward. In this lesson we talk about the formation of these teams and the complex task of directing them.

Introduction

There are various possible structures that can be used to shape the team. Mantei, Weinberg, and Baker are some of the theorists who have addressed these questions, and who have compared the different structures with one another in order to check their effectiveness in different situations. In the following sections we break down some of their most common elements.

The team leader

The head of a work team is a very important figure because this is the person who should lead the group. This person organizes the work to be done and distributes it among the members, encourages and motivates them to work, solves high-level problems, and takes responsibility for the team and the task to be carried out.

When the leader has a good work strategy and is able to organize the group and keep its members motivated, he or she can lead the team in the right direction so that it can complete its work effectively. The leader/head will provide a “why” it has to be done, and the team will provide a “how” it should be done.

Leadership

Leadership is the ability to meet the proposed objectives by directing the team. True leadership consists of a relationship established between the head of the team and the other members, not an “innate talent” of the leader. Its success consists of achieving results with the collaboration of others, so it is not a one-way relationship, but rather a relationship of trust that really works in both directions.

Characteristics of a good leader

A good leader has his or her own characteristics in addition to characteristics as a professional. A good computer specialist is not necessarily a good team leader. We will see, among others:

Leadership styles

A leadership style is the method through which a leader directs, organizes, and motivates people.

Encouraging achievements

This is the ability to optimize a team’s productivity by rewarding initiative and achievements. In addition to financial incentives, there are other forms of motivation. For example, flexible working hours make it possible to reconcile personal, work, and family life. A continuous working day makes it possible to enjoy more leisure time. The choice of days off and holidays helps employees with children select days that coincide with school holidays. Other ways of providing incentives are recognizing achievements so that workers feel their effort is worthwhile, and a good atmosphere that encourages collaboration and trust at work.

Conclusions

Both the head of the team and the other project roles/workers must be properly motivated, and have the appropriate aptitudes and attitudes to develop the project. There are some “good practices” for this, which we can summarize by saying that it is necessary to “lead” more and “command” less.

An interesting analysis is to check how each of the team members deals with change, according to his or her personality, since there are different typologies and aspects of the person are studied, such as emotional intelligence or social skills.

It is the linguistic skill that refers to the interpretation of oral discourse. It is worth remembering that a skill is a way of “using” language and that it is related to the mode of transmission, oral or written, and that, according to the role it plays in communication, it may be receptive or productive in type.

All comprehension, whether listening or reading, is a cognitive process, since the listener/reader relates what he or she already knows or is familiar with to what he or she hears/reads in order to validate or modify a previous approximate “idea”; an idea that had been formed about the new content on the basis of the situation, the topic, etc.

In other words: once physiological, environmental, and code-related issues have been overcome (that is, if there are no problems in the hearing/vision system, if the volume and intensity of the voice are satisfactory/if there is enough light in the case of reading, and if the person has a minimum experience of the language), there will be comprehension if there is confirmation or viability between the previous idea and the new information or, if such confirmation does not exist, there will be comprehension if one proceeds to listen/read again, looking once more for validation or for an attempt to revise the idea in order to move on to an alternative idea.

Synthetic processing of information

When listening, first the noises and non-linguistic sounds that we hear constantly are set aside, so as to pay attention only to the sounds of speech (the brain works here at the phonic level). Then these sounds are identified as phonemes (phonological level) that form words (lexical level), which in turn form phrases (activation of the morphological level), and with the help of morphosyntactic relations, which are the ones that, for example, regulate word order, meaning is given to these phrases (semantic level), and phrase by phrase a coherent text is formed, which is interpreted thanks to or according to the situation (pragmatic level).

Analytical processing of information

When listening, the first things that are understood are the most general aspects of the discourse (the type of text, the communicative situation, the general idea, what is specific to each paragraph), and only afterward are the linguistic units such as phrase or word heard/understood.

The segmentation of the acoustic chain is a micro-skill in which, as in all the others, it is advisable to train students, in order to accustom them to identifying a word within a more extensive series of sounds (identifying a known piece of data within a series of unknown data).

text:
Psychology is a social science, a natural science, and a behavioral science. It is also a professional field with many applications, technologies, and procedures; one of the largest, with numerous groups of professionals in every country. This requires psychologists to be intelligent, creative, flexible, and adaptable in order to achieve a balance that maximizes benefits for society.

The impact of psychology on people’s daily lives, and the ethical dilemmas presented by research and application in this field, require solid and up-to-date preparation. To achieve this, university training programs must be evaluated by considering internal perspectives (what knowledge a student should receive in order to master the basic concepts and theories) and external perspectives (what roles and functions graduating students should be capable of performing).

Another tool that helps ensure the quality of professionals practicing the profession is accreditation, both of educational institutions and individuals (professional certifications) and of the companies or institutions for which they work (for example, through quality schemes such as those associated with ISO 9000 standards). Professional accreditations and certifications should not be a one-time event. They should renew the evaluation through recertification processes.

In addition to initial professional education, psychologists must receive continuous professional training, often facilitated by professional organizations in the different countries. Continuous training shows that the professional remains aware of the latest advances in the profession and is normally a requirement of professional recertification processes.

Psychologists perform a large number of functions. Those specialized in the clinical area provide psychometric assessments, clinical counseling, psychotherapy, and behavioral rehabilitation. Those who work in organizations and industrial settings administer personnel training programs, provide training workshops, training courses, and updating activities in skills related to the management of human resources, especially for those who manage personnel. They also assist in the development of work environments to maximize the motivation and performance of personnel. In communities, psychologists assist with the management of problems such as gangs, the care of abandoned or homeless children, family disintegration, and domestic violence, while in educational institutions they assist in the design of learning programs and the planning of educational goals based on the characteristics of the users.

In all these environments, in the same way as occurs with other specialized professions, psychologists must deal with many prejudices regarding the scope and usefulness of their services. These range from expecting that all of a patient’s personal problems will be solved after a single consultation to demanding a detailed explanation of a complex behavior without giving the professional the opportunity to carry out a detailed analysis of the case. For this reason, an important function of psychologists in their work environment, whatever it may be, is to communicate to others the nature of their profession, the aspects in which it can help, and the things that are outside its scope.

text: In his books and lectures, Manfred Spitzer explains that people do not remember the grammar of their native language through individual cases, but through general (unconscious) rules. To demonstrate this, he has readers and listeners put imaginary words into the past participle, namely a two-syllable word such as “quaffen” and a three-syllable word ending in “-ieren,” such as “flagieren.” He then claims that the result, “gequafft” and “flagiert,” means that words ending in “-ieren” form an exception. But I think this has nothing to do with “-ieren,” and instead purely with the fact that it is a three-syllable word without a prefix. To check this suspicion, however, I would need more genuinely three-syllable verbs, which are rare in German. My question is now: am I right in my suspicion about three-syllable words? Can anyone give me a few examples of genuinely three-syllable verbs that support or refute it? Or is this even stated as a grammar rule in a good grammar book?
