text:
The paper proposes a video prediction model that predicts local transformations rather than future pixels directly. It estimates affine transformations between adjacent frames on a dense grid of overlapping patches, then trains a convolutional network to predict future affine transform fields from past ones. At test time, the predicted transforms are applied to the most recent frame to synthesize future frames. The paper argues that this reduces the blurriness common in pixel-space regression because uncertainty is handled in transformation space, where averaged errors may still produce plausible motion. A second contribution is an evaluation protocol that feeds generated frames into an action classifier trained on real videos, using classification accuracy as a proxy for whether the generated sequence preserves discriminative content. Experiments on moving MNIST and UCF-101 suggest that the method produces sharper outputs than pixel-regression or adversarial baselines and achieves higher downstream classification accuracy, while using far fewer parameters and less computation.

The paper’s main strength is the clarity and simplicity of its central idea. Explicitly modeling local motion is a natural alternative to direct pixel prediction, and the paper gives a concrete version of this idea that is easy to understand. The decomposition into affine transform extraction, transform prediction, and frame reconstruction makes the approach modular. The use of overlapping patches is also sensible: it is more flexible than a single global transform while keeping the prediction target structured and low-dimensional. The unrolled multi-step training procedure is another strength, since it directly addresses the train-test mismatch that occurs when a one-step predictor is applied recursively at test time.

The paper is also useful in stressing that pixel MSE is a poor measure of video prediction quality. This is not a new observation, but the proposed classifier-based evaluation is a practical attempt to define a more task-oriented alternative. The reported gap between ground-truth frames and reconstructions from ground-truth affine transforms is especially informative. It suggests that, at least for the tested frame sizes and patch settings, the affine patch representation preserves much of the information needed by the action classifier. The comparisons to a copy-last-frame baseline, optical flow extrapolation, and a stronger learned video prediction model are also helpful. The method’s computational efficiency is another important advantage. If the reported parameter counts and floating-point operation counts are accurate and comparable, the approach would be an attractive baseline for future work.

I do, however, have several concerns that make the paper less convincing than it could be. The largest issue is that the proposed evaluation protocol, while interesting, is not sufficient by itself to establish video prediction quality. Action classification accuracy on generated frames may reflect preservation of static appearance more than realistic temporal dynamics. The high score of the copy-last-frame baseline, especially when only four generated frames are used, supports this concern. Many UCF-101 classes can be recognized from scene context, objects, clothing, or pose, and the classifier may not be very sensitive to subtle motion artifacts. A model that keeps frames sharp and preserves the actor and background may therefore score well even if it underestimates or distorts motion. The paper acknowledges some underestimation of movement, but the proposed metric may not penalize it enough.

The classifier-based metric also has an ambiguous interpretation. If the goal is to evaluate whether generated videos are plausible continuations, then retaining discriminative features is only one requirement. A generated sequence could preserve the class label while being dynamically implausible, temporally inconsistent, or nearly static. Conversely, a plausible future could change the appearance in a way that makes the classifier less confident, especially for actions that require longer temporal context. The paper would be stronger with additional quantitative measures aimed at temporal realism, such as flow statistics, human preference studies, or classifiers trained to distinguish real from generated sequences. Even a category-level breakdown would help show whether the gains come from motion-sensitive classes or mostly from appearance-dominated ones.

A second concern is the limited depth of the experiments. The moving MNIST results are purely qualitative, and the UCF-101 experiments rely on a single main downstream classifier. There is no statistical analysis or indication of variance across splits, generated samples, or training runs. It is also unclear how sensitive the results are to the affine extraction procedure, which appears to be a critical part of the system. The ablations on patch size, input frames, and prediction horizon are useful, but fairly shallow. For example, the paper reports changes in classification accuracy, but not the reconstruction quality of the affine extraction step, transform prediction error, or the relationship between transform-space MSE and visual quality. Since the method depends on the assumption that local affine transforms are a good representation, that assumption deserves more detailed quantitative support.

The affine transform extractor itself also needs more explanation. The paper says it estimates affine mappings by minimizing reconstruction error, but it does not give enough detail about the optimization procedure, initialization, convergence criteria, boundary handling, regularization, or computational cost. Are the affine transforms estimated independently for every pair of frames in the training set through iterative optimization? If so, how expensive is this preprocessing compared with training a direct prediction model? Are there failure cases when illumination changes, occlusions, or non-rigid deformations lead to poor local affine estimates? Since the learned predictor is trained on these estimated transforms, noise or ambiguity in this stage could have a substantial effect on performance. A fuller description and analysis of this component would improve the paper.

The method also has inherent representational limits that deserve more direct discussion. Applying local transforms to the previous frame cannot synthesize newly visible content, model disocclusions, handle large out-of-plane rotations, or represent appearance changes except through warping. Averaging overlapping transformed patches may reduce some artifacts, but it cannot solve the missing-content problem. This may be acceptable over short horizons, but it should cause degradation over longer predictions. The paper reports results up to eight frames, yet some of the conclusions sound broader than the evidence supports. It would be useful to see how quickly the method fails as the prediction horizon increases, and whether its failures differ qualitatively from those of pixel-space models.

The comparison to prior learned prediction models is promising but not fully satisfying. The paper compares against a multi-scale adversarial model and notes that it is much larger and more expensive. However, it is not entirely clear whether all models were trained under comparable conditions, with the same preprocessing, frame resolution, number of conditioning frames, and prediction horizon. The proposed method predicts transformations extracted from frames, while the baseline predicts pixels, so the training targets and losses are substantially different. That is central to the paper’s argument, but it also makes fairness important. More detail on baseline implementation, hyperparameter tuning, and whether the reported results come from retraining or existing models would make the comparison more credible.

I also find the claim that MSE in transformation space avoids averaging somewhat overstated. The paper itself notes that the model underestimates movement, which is an averaging effect. Predicting the mean of plausible transformations may produce a sharp frame because the previous image is warped rather than regressed, but it can still produce an implausible or overly conservative trajectory. This distinction matters. The approach avoids pixel blurring caused by averaging in image space, but it does not avoid uncertainty averaging in general. If multiple futures are possible, a deterministic MSE-trained transform predictor still has the usual conditional mean problem. Modeling a distribution over transformations, as the conclusion mentions, seems important rather than merely an optional extension.

I have several specific questions for the authors. How are the affine transforms estimated in practice, and how long does this preprocessing take on UCF-101? Do the reported computational savings cover only the prediction network, or do they include affine extraction for conditioning frames at test time? How sensitive is the method to the stride and overlap used in patch reconstruction? Does the classifier-based evaluation use only generated frames, or are the conditioning frames also included as classifier input? If conditioning frames are excluded, how are short clips aligned with the classifier’s expected temporal input? If they are included, how much of the classification accuracy comes from the real conditioning frames rather than the generated continuation? Can the authors report category-level accuracies, especially for actions where temporal motion is essential? Finally, can they provide quantitative results for longer horizons, even if performance degrades, to clarify the useful operating range of the method?

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially useful, especially as a strong and efficient baseline for short-term video prediction. The idea of predicting local transformations is intuitive, well motivated, and produces sharper outputs than direct pixel regression. The proposed evaluation protocol is also a worthwhile contribution because it moves beyond pixel MSE. At the same time, the empirical case is not fully convincing. The evaluation may reward preservation of appearance more than realistic motion, the affine extraction stage is under-specified, and the method’s limitations for occlusion, disocclusion, and long-term prediction are not quantified well enough. My recommendation is therefore borderline, leaning weak reject in its current form. With a more rigorous evaluation of temporal realism, clearer implementation details, and stronger baseline comparisons, this could become a compelling contribution.

text:
The paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework for solving combinatorial optimization problems with neural networks. It focuses mainly on the Euclidean traveling salesman problem, with a shorter demonstration on Knapsack. The core idea is to use a pointer-network-style recurrent model as a stochastic policy over permutations, train it with policy gradients using tour length as the reward signal, and improve inference either by sampling many candidate tours or by using “active search,” where the policy parameters are further optimized on a single test instance. The paper argues that this removes the need for supervised optimal labels, allows the model to learn useful heuristics from reward alone, and offers a fairly general recipe for neural approaches to combinatorial search. Empirically, the method improves substantially over a supervised pointer network baseline and reaches near-optimal results on random 2D Euclidean TSP instances up to 100 nodes when given extensive sampling or test-time optimization.

This is an interesting and timely paper. Its main contribution is not that it competes with specialized TSP solvers; the authors are clear that it does not. Rather, it shows a plausible way to train neural combinatorial policies directly against an optimization objective instead of imitating an external solver. That distinction matters. Supervised learning from solver outputs can be brittle, costly to scale to new problems, and not fully aligned with the real objective, since reproducing one particular tour is not the same as finding any short tour. Reinforcement learning is a natural framing here, and the results suggest that it makes a real difference: the RL-trained policies outperform the supervised pointer-network approach by a wide margin. The active search component is also appealing. Combinatorial optimization at test time is, by nature, a search problem, and the paper shows that gradient-based adaptation of a neural policy can serve as a form of instance-specific search.

Another strength is that the empirical presentation is fairly open about the method’s limitations. The authors compare against exact and heuristic TSP solvers and state clearly that their approach is much slower than Concorde or strong local search methods. This makes the paper more credible. The comparisons with Christofides-style heuristics, generic OR tools, and optimal solutions give useful context for judging where the learned method stands. The percentile plots of tour length ratios are especially helpful, since averages alone can hide whether a method is consistently near-optimal or succeeds only on some instances. The paper also tests several inference settings, including greedy decoding, ensembling, sampling, active search from a pretrained policy, and active search from scratch. This helps separate the value of the learned initialization from the effect of spending more computation at test time.

The paper is also important because it points toward a broader research direction. The proposed architecture and training procedure suggest that neural networks can learn reusable construction heuristics for structured discrete problems. A pointer mechanism is a sensible choice for problems whose solutions are permutations or subsets of inputs. Although the Knapsack experiment is less developed than the TSP section, it supports the claim that the approach is not entirely specific to tours. The discussion of feasibility constraints and penalties is useful as well, and shows that the authors recognize the difficulties involved in extending the method to more constrained combinatorial settings.

The paper does have several important weaknesses. The most serious is that the evidence for general combinatorial optimization remains narrow. The main experiments use random Euclidean TSP instances with points sampled uniformly in the unit square. This is a standard and convenient distribution, but it is much simpler than many real routing problems and may strongly favor models that learn geometric regularities. It is unclear how well the learned policy transfers to non-uniform point distributions, clustered instances, non-Euclidean metrics, asymmetric TSP, or instances with additional constraints. Since the paper emphasizes generality and reduced heuristic engineering, the evaluation should test distribution shift more directly. A policy trained on uniform random TSP instances may be learning a distribution-specific geometric prior rather than a broadly useful optimization strategy.

A second major weakness is computational efficiency. The best results depend on sampling or active search over very large numbers of candidate solutions, with reported runtimes that are orders of magnitude worse than specialized solvers and often worse than reasonably generic local search. This does not undermine the research contribution, but it does weaken the practical framing. If a method needs 1.28 million sampled tours or many thousands of gradient updates for each test instance, it is hard to view it as an effective solver rather than an interesting proof of concept. The paper would benefit from a more careful analysis of the tradeoff between computation and solution quality, especially against simple baselines that also improve with test-time budget, such as randomized 2-opt, repeated nearest-neighbor starts, or local improvement applied to neural samples. The comparison to OR tools is useful, but the neural method’s apparent advantage over some generic baselines may vanish under equal wall-clock time or equal candidate-evaluation budgets.

The active search method is intriguing but not fully explained. Optimizing the policy on a single instance from sampled rewards resembles a learned stochastic local search procedure, but the paper does not analyze enough why it works, when it fails, or what role the pretrained policy plays beyond initializing the search near good tours. For TSP50, sampling appears competitive with, or better than, active search, while for TSP100 active search helps more. This difference deserves explanation. Does active search work mainly by reducing entropy around promising regions, by learning instance-specific geometric structure, or by acting like an adaptive sampling temperature? How sensitive is it to learning rate, baseline decay, batch size, number of glimpses, and input shuffling? Since active search is one of the paper’s distinctive ideas, stronger ablations and diagnostics would make the contribution clearer.

The supervised baseline also raises concerns. The authors say that their supervised implementation trained on optimal tours performs worse than results reported in earlier work, and that learning from optimal tours may be harder because of subtle features. This is plausible, but not fully satisfying. Since one of the main empirical claims is that RL improves substantially over supervised learning, the supervised baseline should be as strong and carefully tuned as possible. It would be useful to compare supervised pretraining followed by RL fine-tuning, imitation of multiple optimal or near-optimal tours when symmetries exist, and supervised training with the same search procedures used for the RL policy. Without these controls, it is difficult to tell whether the improvement comes from reinforcement learning itself, from differences in the training setup, or from test-time sampling and optimization.

The claims about generality should also be moderated. The pointer network architecture fits problems where the model selects elements from an input sequence, especially when feasibility can be enforced by masking already selected items. Many combinatorial optimization problems, however, involve richer state-dependent constraints, graph structures, or solution representations that are not naturally captured by a sequence-to-sequence model over input indices. The discussion of penalties for infeasible solutions is reasonable but still speculative. In problems where feasible solutions are rare, simple penalty methods may lead to extremely sparse or uninformative rewards. The Knapsack result helps, but Knapsack is still relatively simple compared with vehicle routing with time windows, graph coloring, scheduling, or integer programming. Evidence on a constrained problem where feasibility is genuinely difficult would better support the broad framing.

Several points would benefit from clarification. How robust are the trained TSP policies to changes in the test distribution, such as clustered cities, non-square domains, mixtures of distributions, or larger graph sizes than those used in training? How much of the gain from active search depends on random shuffling of the input sequence, and does performance vary significantly with input ordering under greedy decoding? When using 1.28 million samples, how many distinct tours are produced, and how concentrated is the policy distribution before and after active search? An equal-time comparison against simple randomized local-search baselines would also be valuable, especially if local improvement were initialized from the model’s own tours. That hybrid baseline would show whether the neural network is most useful as a generator of good starting solutions rather than as a complete solver. For Knapsack, more detail is needed on the instance distributions, capacities, item value and weight distributions, and comparisons to dynamic programming or greedy baselines. The claim of optimality up to 200 items is encouraging, but hard to interpret without this information.

The ablation study could also be expanded. The critic architecture, number of glimpses, logit clipping, temperature tuning, model size, and batch size all seem potentially important. Since policy-gradient methods can be unstable and sensitive to variance reduction, it would help to know which components are essential. For example, how much worse is a moving-average baseline than the learned critic during pretraining? Does increasing the number of glimpses improve TSP100 while slowing inference? Does the model learn meaningful geometric behavior, such as avoiding crossings, and if so, when does this emerge during training? Visualizing failure cases could strengthen the paper, especially by comparing greedy decoding with sampling and active search.

Overall, my recommendation is weak accept. The method is not competitive with mature combinatorial optimization solvers in speed, scale, or final solution quality, and the evaluation is limited mainly to uniform random Euclidean TSP. Even so, the paper presents a clear and promising formulation of neural combinatorial optimization as reinforcement learning, shows a substantial improvement over supervised pointer-network training, and introduces active search as an interesting bridge between learned policies and instance-specific optimization. The work is likely to encourage further research on learned heuristics, neural construction policies, and hybrid neural-search methods. I would be more enthusiastic if the paper included stronger distribution-shift experiments, more rigorous equal-compute baselines, and a deeper analysis of active search, but it still makes a worthwhile conceptual and empirical contribution.

text:
The paper proposes compositional kernel machines, an instance-based method for visual classification that aims to combine features of kernel methods, nearest-neighbor methods, and convolutional architectures. The main idea is to compare a query image not only with the training images themselves, but also with a very large implicit set of “virtual instances” created by recombining local elements from those training examples. To make inference over this exponential set tractable, the authors use a sum-product-function representation under decomposability constraints. They define CKMs recursively through leaf kernels, products over disjoint scopes, and weighted sums over common scopes. They also describe a uniform-weight version and a discriminatively trained version using leave-one-out squared-hinge loss. Experiments on small NORB and two derived NORB variants suggest that the approach can outperform standard instance-based methods and compete with some neural baselines in low-data settings where composition and symmetry matter.

The paper’s main strength is that it explores a useful middle ground between classical nonparametric or kernel methods and deep compositional models. The motivation is convincing: if visual categories are compositional and show local symmetries, then a method that can recombine observed parts should need fewer complete image examples than a purely global nearest-neighbor or SVM approach. Sum-product structure is a natural way to represent many possible recombinations compactly, and it could be powerful. I also appreciated the authors’ effort to make the sample-complexity argument concrete. Rather than only claiming that composition should help, they implement a model that can sum or maximize over many latent part assignments and test it on settings designed to isolate composition and symmetry.

The paper is also fairly clear at the conceptual level. Defining CKMs as recursively composed sums and products is simple, and the analogy to sum-product networks and image grammars is helpful. The claim that SVMs and nearest-neighbor-like methods can be viewed as special cases helps position the work. The leave-one-out training objective makes sense for an instance-based learner, and the distinction between CKM with uniform weights and CKMW with learned weights is useful in the experiments. The paper is ambitious: it tries to introduce a family of models rather than a single ad hoc architecture.

The experiments provide some encouraging evidence. The gains over raw nearest-neighbor methods on small NORB support the claim that local composition can reduce the curse of dimensionality relative to global image matching. The synthetic NORB Compositions experiment is a reasonable attempt to test whether a method can generalize from observed parts to unseen combinations. In that setting, the reported advantage over a conventionally trained convolutional network is plausible and interesting, especially given the small training set. The NORB Symmetries learning curves also tell a coherent story: the proposed method benefits from additional examples without requiring extensive retraining, and the learned-weight version begins to improve as more data become available.

I still have several serious concerns that keep me from being convinced by the paper in its current form. One concern is that the term “kernel machine” is used rather loosely. The theoretical presentation starts from kernel methods and kernel composition, but the experimental model uses a max-sum semiring and arbitrary local scoring functions, including costs and thresholds. It is unclear whether the resulting discriminant corresponds to a positive semidefinite kernel, or whether the method is better understood as a latent structured matching model. This matters because part of the paper’s motivation rests on the training advantages of kernel machines, while the optimization objective is later described as generally nonconvex. If CKMs are mainly max-product latent-composition models, then their relationship to SVMs is more limited than the framing implies.

The theoretical contribution also feels underdeveloped. The sum-product theorem shows that a decomposable sum-product function can be evaluated in time linear in its size, but this property comes from the representation rather than from a new algorithm specific to CKMs. The more important question is how large the representation must be to capture useful visual compositions. The experimental architecture includes unary and pairwise max nodes over ORB features, while the equations suggest potentially very large pairwise maximizations over all training elements. The paper mentions approximate nearest-neighbor structures and pruning, but the exact computational complexity of the implemented model is not transparent enough. The claim that the method sums over exponentially many virtual instances is formally true for decomposable structures, but it may overstate the practical modeling power if the architecture captures only limited local pairwise structure.

The empirical evidence is narrow, and some comparisons do not seem fully fair to the baselines. All experiments use NORB or constructed variants of NORB. NORB is useful for controlled studies, but it is small and stylized, while the paper makes broad claims about object recognition and alternatives to convolutional networks. The convolutional baselines are not described in enough detail to judge their strength. For example, on the NORB Compositions task, the convnet performs near chance, but this could reflect an unsuitable architecture, insufficient augmentation, or a weak training protocol rather than a fundamental limitation. The comparison to an SVM using features from a pretrained Inception model is also awkward, since those features come from a very different image distribution and may be poorly matched to grayscale toy images. In the small NORB comparison, some numbers come from prior work and others from the authors’ own implementation, which makes it hard to separate algorithmic gains from differences in preprocessing, feature extraction, and hyperparameter tuning.

The synthetic datasets raise additional questions. The NORB Compositions task is interesting, but it may strongly favor local feature matching. If the label is determined by the identity of local toy instances in an image, and ORB descriptors can match those instances directly, then the task may be closer to multi-object instance retrieval than to semantic compositional generalization. That is still a valid problem, but it is narrower than the discussion suggests. It would help to know how the method behaves when the relevant parts vary more, when distractors are present, or when local descriptors are less reliable. The NORB Symmetries experiment also seems well suited to an ORB-based method, since ORB descriptors already provide some rotation invariance. The paper should separate the gains due to the CKM composition mechanism from those due to hand-engineered invariances in the local features.

The learning procedure needs more detail and evaluation. The leave-one-out objective is appealing, but it is unclear how expensive exact training is as the number of images and elements grows, especially with pairwise terms. The authors say that gradients can be computed efficiently and that small leaf-kernel values may be excluded, but the experiments do not clearly distinguish exact training from approximate training. There is little discussion of regularization, constraints on weights, initialization beyond uniform weights, or sensitivity to hyperparameters. The method includes ORB extraction parameters, leaf-kernel parameters, cost-function parameters, approximate search parameters, and architectural parameters, so a more systematic analysis is needed. The paper criticizes convolutional networks for difficult hyperparameter tuning, but CKMs seem to introduce a substantial design space of their own.

Scalability is another concern. The paper argues that CKMs are attractive when new data arrive because training can be fast and instance-based. However, the model size grows with the training set, and test-time computation appears much slower than the reported convolutional network testing time. This tradeoff may be acceptable in some settings, but the paper should be more precise about memory use, indexing costs, update costs, and test-time latency as datasets grow beyond NORB scale. The claim that adding instances and categories is easy should be supported by incremental experiments, not just stated. For real object recognition tasks, storing and searching all local features from all training images could become a serious bottleneck.

I would like the authors to clarify several points. In what precise sense is the experimental CKM a kernel machine? Does the max-sum version define a positive semidefinite kernel, or is it better viewed as a latent matching discriminant? How much of the empirical improvement comes from ORB features alone, local position-aware matching, the pairwise source-image coherence cost, and the sum-product architecture? Ablations removing each of these components would be valuable. The paper should also explain how hyperparameters are selected, and whether validation images are disjoint from test images in object identity and transformation. For the pairwise max nodes, is the maximization over all pairs of training elements actually performed, approximated by nearest-neighbor search, or pruned by thresholds? What are the memory and runtime costs as functions of the number of training images and extracted elements? Finally, the method should be evaluated on at least one less controlled dataset, or against a stronger modern convnet baseline trained with a protocol suited to small data.

Overall, I find the paper creative and potentially promising, but not yet convincing as a strong ICLR contribution. The idea of implicit compositional virtual instances is interesting, and the connection to tractable sum-product evaluation could lead to useful models. In its current form, however, the submission overstates the kernel-method interpretation, relies on limited and somewhat favorable experiments, and lacks enough ablation and scalability analysis to establish the practical value of the approach. My recommendation is weak reject for the main conference. I would be enthusiastic about a revised version with clearer theoretical positioning, stronger baselines, more detailed computational analysis, and broader empirical validation.

text:
The paper addresses the problem of answering long, non-factoid questions, focusing on love-advice questions from a Japanese community QA service. The proposed system has two main parts. It first learns word embeddings influenced by document-level semantic information, such as question categories and title terms, so that words like “relationship” can carry different relevance in different topical contexts. It then builds an answer by selecting and combining shorter sentence units of predefined types, such as a conclusion and a supplement, rather than choosing an entire existing answer. The model represents questions and candidate answer sentences with bidirectional LSTMs, uses a hinge-loss objective over correct and incorrect sentence combinations, and applies attention from the selected conclusion sentence to the supplemental sentence. Experiments on Oshiete goo data suggest improvements over LSTM-based answer selection baselines, especially in the harder answer construction setting, and the authors report deployment in a live love-advice service.

The paper takes on an interesting and practically important problem. Non-factoid QA is a setting where selecting an answer from a fixed archive is often not enough, and the paper is right to stress that advice questions require sensitivity to situation, tone, and discourse structure. Moving from whole-answer retrieval to sentence-level composition is a reasonable middle ground between retrieval and full neural generation. This is especially sensible for advice domains, where fully generative systems can produce fluent but unsafe, generic, or incoherent content. By limiting the output to human-authored sentence fragments and a predefined rhetorical structure, the system may offer more control than unconstrained generation.

Another strength is the paper’s attention to domain-dependent word usage. Using category and title information as semantic context for representation learning is simple but plausible, and it addresses a real weakness of generic embeddings in community QA data. The paper gives a clear motivation: some words become important only within a particular category, while others are common across many categories and should not dominate matching. The comparison between the ordinary LSTM baseline and the semantic-embedding variant suggests that this component helps performance.

The answer construction setup is also appealing at a high level. The authors observe that answers in a domain such as love advice often follow a recognizable discourse pattern, and they use this to break answer production into the selection of sentences with specific roles. This is a useful engineering insight. The joint objective, which considers both question-sentence relevance and sentence-sentence compatibility, is better than selecting the best conclusion and best supplement independently. The attention mechanism from the conclusion to the supplement is also appropriate in principle, since the supplement should elaborate on the same topic or rationale as the conclusion.

The practical focus of the work is another positive point. The paper uses data from a real QA service, works with a non-English dataset, and reports not only offline metrics but also some human judgments and deployment statistics. Many QA papers rely on clean benchmark data and say little about how a system behaves with real users. The attempt to deploy the model and collect user feedback makes the work potentially valuable.

However, several weaknesses limit the paper in its current form. The most important issue is that the contribution is overstated as “answer generation.” The system does not generate new sentences. It retrieves and recombines sentence fragments extracted from existing answers according to a manually specified scenario. This is a legitimate task, but it should be described more accurately as answer construction or sentence-level answer composition. The introduction repeatedly contrasts the method with answer selection and presents it as moving beyond selection, yet the system remains fundamentally extractive. The paper would be stronger if it defined the task as constrained extractive answer composition and discussed its limits compared with genuine generation.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. The main offline construction metric measures whether the model can recreate original conclusion-supplement pairs. This is a narrow proxy for answer quality. A constructed answer can be useful even if it does not match the original pair, and the original pair may not be the only good answer to a question. Average precision over exact or annotated original pairs may therefore misrepresent the task. At the same time, because many candidate sentences may be generic advice statements, the metric may reward superficial matching. The paper needs a clearer account of what counts as a correct constructed answer, how many gold combinations exist per question, and whether correctness is judged semantically or by identity with extracted sentences.

The human evaluation is promising but underdescribed. The paper reports judgments by two experts, but it does not clearly state how the questions were sampled, whether the experts were blind to system identity, how disagreements were resolved, or what the inter-annotator agreement was. The four-point rating scale is reasonable, but the evaluation appears to compare only the proposed method with one baseline, rather than with all relevant variants. It also lacks human-written answers as an upper bound. Without these details, the reported improvement is hard to interpret. The deployment figure that 455 out of 1,492 answers were judged “Good” is interesting, but it is not a controlled evaluation and may reflect user expectations, interface effects, or selection bias.

The baselines and ablations are incomplete. The paper compares against LSTM answer selection and variants of the proposed method, but not against simpler retrieval or composition methods that might be strong. Useful baselines would include selecting conclusions and supplements independently with BM25, TF-IDF, or embedding similarity; retrieving the best original answer and extracting its first conclusion-like and supplement-like sentences; or using a learned pairwise ranker with handcrafted lexical features. The paper claims that the model avoids bad sentence combinations, but a direct comparison to a two-stage system would help: first retrieve relevant conclusions, then rank supplements by compatibility. The current ablations also do not cleanly isolate the effects of the semantic embeddings, joint loss, pretraining, and attention.

The dataset description raises concerns. The answer construction corpus contains about 5,000 question-conclusion-supplement examples, which is fairly small for training several LSTM models. The paper says that conclusions and supplements were extracted by human experts, while also suggesting that sentence extraction methods could be used. Since the model depends on these sentence-type labels, the annotation process is central and should be described in more detail. How were sentence types defined? Were multiple conclusions or supplements allowed per answer? How consistent were annotators? Were candidate sentence pools limited to love-advice questions or drawn from all categories? Were near-duplicate questions or answers present across train and test folds? Because the data comes from a community QA site, duplicate or templated answers could inflate performance if not controlled.

The model presentation is sometimes unclear. The semantic embedding method is described as averaging category and title vectors with context word vectors, but the exact training objective, window size, negative sampling or softmax details, and use of category/title information at inference time are not fully specified. In the answer construction model, the notation for the loss and representations is difficult to follow. The margin parameter k is said to satisfy 0 < k < 1, but the experimental section sets k to 1.0. The loss includes several terms comparing combinations with one or both incorrect components, but it is unclear how negative conclusions and supplements are sampled, whether hard negatives are used, and how sensitive the results are to this choice. The attention mechanism also appears to compute unnormalized weights independently for each supplement token; the authors should clarify whether the weights are normalized across time and, if not, why this formulation is preferable.

The paper also needs a discussion of safety and appropriateness. A system that gives love advice to real users may affect emotionally vulnerable people. Even if the domain seems casual, questions may involve harassment, abuse, self-harm, coercion, age differences, or other sensitive situations. Recombining human-authored sentences can still produce harmful or inappropriate advice when those sentences are taken out of context. The paper should discuss filtering, moderation, fallback behavior, and whether the predefined scenario is enough to prevent unsafe recommendations. This matters especially because the authors emphasize deployment.

Several points need clarification. What exactly is the candidate pool at test time: extracted conclusion and supplement sentences from the training set, the full QA archive, or a held-out candidate set? Are sentences from the same original answer as the test question removed to prevent leakage? How many candidate conclusions and supplements are ranked per question, and how is the search over all possible pairs made tractable? How are title tokens used for a new user question if the title is absent or noisy? Does the semantic embedding method require the correct category at test time, and what happens if the category is wrong? In the human evaluation, were judges blind, how many questions were evaluated, and what was the inter-annotator agreement? It would also help to see failure cases, especially cases where the conclusion is plausible but the supplement changes the intended meaning or leads to socially inappropriate advice.

Overall, the paper addresses an important and underexplored problem with a practical and intuitively sensible approach. Constructing non-factoid answers from typed sentence units is worth studying, and the domain-specific embedding component is a reasonable addition. Still, the paper overstates the generative nature of the system, does not specify the dataset and annotation process in enough detail, and relies on an evaluation that is not strong enough to establish answer quality. The gains are encouraging, but the lack of strong non-neural and two-stage baselines, limited human evaluation details, and unclear safety controls weaken the contribution. My recommendation is weak reject. I would be more positive about a revised version that frames the task more accurately, provides a rigorous blind human evaluation with agreement statistics, includes stronger retrieval and composition baselines with clearer ablations, and gives a fuller account of data construction and deployment safeguards.

text:
The paper proposes an iterative refinement method for machine translation. Instead of generating a translation once from left to right, the system starts with a complete translation and repeatedly edits it by substituting individual words. The motivation is that standard left-to-right or bottom-up decoders commit to earlier choices and cannot easily revisit them. A refinement model, by contrast, can condition on both the source sentence and the entire current hypothesis. The authors begin with a word-level error detection model, then introduce a convolutional attention-based model that predicts a replacement word at each target position from the source and surrounding target context. They then extend it to a dual-attention model that also attends to the initial translation. At test time, the model proposes substitutions for all positions, a heuristic or classifier scores the edits, and the highest-scoring edit is applied until a threshold is met or a maximum number of edits is reached. On WMT15 German-English, starting from a phrase-based MT system, the best method improves BLEU by about 0.3–0.4 across several test sets while changing fewer than one word per sentence on average.

The main appeal of the paper is its clear treatment of translation refinement as a separate decoding paradigm. Rather than treating translation as a strictly generative left-to-right process, the authors study a model that can see a complete candidate output and revise local decisions. This is a natural and potentially important direction. Many translation errors become visible only after later context has been generated, and a model with access to both left and right context may be better suited to fixing agreement, lexical choice, punctuation, and local semantic errors. The paper is also concrete. The models are easy to understand, the refinement procedure is explicit, and the experiments cover useful variants, including single-source attention, dual attention, different scoring heuristics, and oracle analyses.

The paper also avoids relying on manually post-edited data. The models are trained from parallel data and system-generated hypotheses, which makes the approach more scalable than automatic post-editing setups that require human corrections of machine output. The procedure for generating initial guesses on the training set is carefully designed: the authors use multiple phrase-based systems trained on disjoint subsets, which helps avoid the unrealistic case where the baseline system translates sentences it has already seen during training. This is an important experimental detail and makes the reported improvements more credible.

The dual-attention model is a sensible extension. By conditioning not only on the source and reference-side context during training, but also on the system’s current guess, it reduces the mismatch between training and testing and gives the model a way to copy words that are already correct. The reported drop in perplexity from the single-attention model to the dual-attention model is convincing evidence that the guess translation carries useful information. The finding that the dual model is more conservative also fits the task: when the starting point is a strong baseline, most words should remain unchanged, and a refinement model must avoid unnecessary edits. The examples show that the model can correct meaningful lexical errors, punctuation, tense, and pronoun choices.

The oracle experiments are useful as well. They show that the model’s proposed substitutions contain more potential improvement than the deployed heuristic can extract, and that deciding when and where to edit is a major bottleneck. This separates two questions: whether the word prediction model can suggest useful alternatives, and whether the refinement strategy can reliably choose beneficial substitutions. The gap between the heuristic method and the oracle suggests that the approach still has room to improve, rather than having reached a hard limit.

The empirical contribution, however, is modest in its current form. The best reported gain is only about 0.4 BLEU, with mean gains of roughly 0.32 BLEU over the WMT test sets. The consistency across test sets is encouraging, but the size of the gains is small, and the paper does not report statistical significance testing. Given the known variance of BLEU when outputs differ only slightly, it is hard to judge whether the gains are robust enough to justify the added modeling and decoding complexity. The method changes only about 0.6 words per sentence, which is interesting, but it also limits the overall effect. The paper would be stronger with significance tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, or a more detailed breakdown of which edits contribute to the BLEU gains.

The restriction to word substitutions is a major limitation. Many translation errors require insertions, deletions, phrase-level replacements, reordering, or changes in segmentation. Several examples show this problem directly: the model sometimes replaces a word because it cannot insert a missing function word or restructure a phrase, which leads to output that is unnatural or only partly improved. Since the paper motivates the method as a form of human-like revision, a one-for-one substitution operation makes the refinement process much less expressive than the motivation suggests. The authors mention this as future work, but the limitation affects the central claim. It is unclear whether a substitution-only model can scale beyond minor lexical cleanup.

The comparison setting is also narrow. The method is evaluated only on German-to-English and only on top of a phrase-based translation system. By 2017, neural machine translation systems are already strong baselines, and the paper’s motivation partly concerns neural left-to-right decoding. It would be important to evaluate refinement on a neural baseline, or at least explain why phrase-based output is the main test case. Phrase-based systems have different error profiles from neural systems, and a model trained to fix PBMT output may mainly learn to repair local lexical and fluency errors. It remains unclear whether the approach would help strong attention-based neural systems, whose errors may be more global, more fluent but semantically wrong, or related to omissions. Experiments with weaker initial guesses, stronger initial guesses, or multiple guess translations would also help clarify when iterative refinement is useful.

The paper could do more to distinguish the work from automatic post-editing and confidence estimation. The authors note that their method does not require post-edited data, but it still resembles monolingual or bilingual post-editing of MT output with a neural model. The discussion would be stronger if it positioned the method more clearly against prior work on system combination, rescoring, lattice or n-best list refinement, and post-editing trained from synthetic data. If the baseline system can produce n-best lists or lattices, a strong rescoring or minimum-risk decoding baseline might capture some of the same corrections without a separate iterative editing procedure. Without such comparisons, it is hard to tell whether the proposed decoding scheme is the best way to use this information.

The edit selection mechanism is another weak point. The authors test simple confidence heuristics and a small classifier, but the classifier appears to use only two log-probability features. That seems too limited for deciding whether an edit improves translation quality. Features such as position, source attention entropy, local language model scores, lexical identity, edit type, baseline confidence, and sentence-level context are ignored. Since the oracle analysis shows that edit selection is a major bottleneck, the paper should either include a stronger learned selection model or frame the current results more clearly as preliminary. It is also unclear how well the thresholds and maximum edit counts would generalize across domains, language pairs, and baseline systems.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on BLEU. Because the system makes very few substitutions, BLEU may reward edits that move the output closer to the single reference even when they do not improve adequacy or fluency, and it may miss valid improvements that are not reflected in the reference. The error detection section itself notes the problem of single-reference evaluation, but the final evaluation does not address it. A human evaluation or a targeted analysis of accepted and rejected edits would help. For example, what fraction of edits improve adequacy, improve fluency, act as neutral paraphrases, or harm the translation? Are the gains mostly from punctuation and morphology, or do they include substantive lexical corrections? Do repeated edits ever cause oscillations or degradation? These details would make the contribution more convincing.

I have several questions for the authors. How sensitive are the results to the strength and type of the initial translation system? Would the same refinement model improve a neural MT baseline, or does it mainly correct artifacts of phrase-based translation? Were the BLEU gains tested for statistical significance on each test set and on the concatenation of all test sets? How often does the model propose the identity substitution, and how often are proposed substitutions rejected by the threshold? What is the runtime cost of iterative refinement relative to baseline decoding? Does the model ever cycle between alternatives across iterations, and if so, how is that handled? Why does the learned classifier not outperform the simple product heuristic, and were richer features tried? Finally, can the authors provide an edit-type analysis showing which substitution categories account for most of the BLEU improvement?

Overall, I find the idea promising and the paper well written, but the empirical evidence is not yet fully convincing. The work gives a clean and interesting formulation of iterative translation refinement, and the consistent small gains suggest that the method is doing something meaningful. At the same time, the improvements are very small, the edit space is limited, the baselines are narrow, and the evaluation does not show that the method is broadly useful beyond minor corrections to phrase-based output. My recommendation is a weak reject in its current form. I would be more positive with stronger comparisons, significance testing, evaluation on neural baselines, and either a better edit selection model or a broader edit space.

text:
The paper asks whether a convolutional network trained with weak labels on rendered tic-tac-toe boards can learn representations that correspond to game concepts such as board locations, legal turns, and winning moves. The authors generate all legal tic-tac-toe states in which one player can win on the next move, render those states as images, and assign one of 18 labels indicating the winning side and square. They then train an AlexNet-style classifier with global average pooling and inspect class activation maps. They find that the CAMs often highlight the empty square where the winning move should be played, even though the model never receives pixel-level localization labels. The paper also tests variants with grid lines and altered piece appearances, and proposes two quantitative measures meant to capture whether the activation map identifies the correct move. The authors take these results as evidence that game concepts can emerge under weak supervision, that cross-modal supervision can extend to higher-level action or game-rule semantics, and that CAMs can activate on non-salient image regions.

The central idea is appealing. Tic-tac-toe is small enough to enumerate exhaustively, but it still has relational structure: rows, columns, diagonals, turns, two players, and win conditions. A controlled domain like this is a reasonable way to study representation learning, visualization, and weak supervision without the confounds of large natural-image datasets. The qualitative observation that activation maps can peak on empty board squares is also interesting. It shows that discriminative spatial evidence in a CNN does not have to coincide with object texture or local visual salience; it can come from contextual information in the receptive field. The paper is clearly motivated and tries to connect the experiment to broader questions in deep reinforcement learning, cross-modal supervision, and interpretability. The authors also deserve credit for proposing quantitative measures instead of relying only on selected visual examples, and for including controls based on appearance changes and an intermediate-training analysis.

That said, the main claims are much stronger than the evidence supports. The largest problem is that the supervision is not as weak as the paper suggests. The 18 labels correspond directly to the player and square of the winning next move. The model is not given a segmentation mask or an explicit rule table, but the class label still encodes the answer to the localization and action-selection problem. In this setting, a CAM that highlights the square associated with a class is not strong evidence that the network has discovered a game concept in the sense of understanding a rule. It may simply have learned discriminative visual templates associated with each of the 18 output classes. Because the task is limited to positions where the game ends in one move, the input-output mapping can be solved by recognizing local or semi-local patterns of pieces, without representing the full rules of tic-tac-toe.

For this reason, the paper’s use of the term “concepts” is problematic. Claims that the network learns the concept of the grid, the winning rule, or the two sides require stronger behavioral evidence. If a representation encodes the winning rule, it should transfer to states where the best move blocks an opponent, creates a fork, or avoids a trap. It should generalize across board transformations or to different board sizes. It should support accurate play beyond immediate wins, or allow a simple downstream model to infer legal and winning moves in held-out configurations. The current experiment considers only a narrow subset of positions and evaluates whether the most active region matches the location already encoded in the class label. That is closer to weakly supervised localization of a class-correlated square than to concept learning.

A second major concern is the lack of clarity about train/test separation and generalization. The paper reports 100% classification accuracy on the tic-tac-toe dataset, but it is unclear whether this is training accuracy, validation accuracy, or accuracy on a held-out set of states. The dataset contains only 1029 samples for the main task and is generated synthetically from a small finite state space, so memorization is a real possibility. The localization scores are also not described in enough detail to tell whether they are computed on training examples or held-out examples. If all CAM visualizations and RAC/RCO scores are measured on the same examples used for fine-tuning, they provide only weak evidence of learned structure. A convincing study would need held-out board states, perhaps held-out board symmetries, and controls designed to separate rule learning from associations between visual templates and labels.

The paper also relies too heavily on CAM as evidence of internal understanding. CAM shows class-discriminative spatial contributions under a particular architecture; it is not a direct readout of semantic concepts. A highlighted empty square may appear because the feature at that spatial location has a receptive field covering the relevant row, column, or diagonal, not because the model represents “this is the winning move” in a meaningful conceptual sense. That would still be an interesting visualization result, but it should be framed more cautiously. The paper also does not compare CAM with other attribution methods, occlusion tests, gradient-based saliency, or direct probes of intermediate features. Without such controls, it is hard to know whether the heatmaps reflect robust model reasoning or artifacts of the visualization method, rendering geometry, receptive field layout, padding, or class-specific templates.

Several baselines would strengthen the experimental design. A linear classifier or multilayer perceptron on symbolic 3-by-3 board encodings would establish the intrinsic difficulty of the classification task. A CNN trained from scratch, rather than fine-tuned from ImageNet AlexNet, would test whether pretraining matters in this synthetic setting. A model trained with randomly permuted labels, or with labels that encode only the side but not the square, would help show whether CAM localization is genuinely tied to game structure. A simple pattern-matching baseline, or a non-convolutional classifier that chooses the square, would put the RAC values in context. Because the board states are tiny and discrete, the paper should also address whether the CNN is exploiting absolute position and fixed rendering conventions rather than learning a reusable rule.

The quantitative evaluation is not yet convincing. Representation accuracy is intuitive, but the definition of “most activated patch” depends on map resolution, interpolation, patch size, and tie-breaking, and these details are missing. Representation consistency is harder to interpret. The reported values are negative and scaled by 10^3, but the meaning of those values is not explained. If higher consistency means better alignment with an ideal activation map, the table should say so clearly and should report confidence intervals, or at least variation across random initializations. The improvements from adding grid lines are plausible, but the paper attributes them to the network being given an implied board concept. A simpler explanation is that grid lines provide strong spatial anchors and high-frequency gradients at fixed positions, making localization by CAM easier. That is not necessarily evidence of a more semantic representation.

The link to cross-modal supervision is also weak. In these experiments, the labels are generated by a simulator from the same underlying board state that is rendered as an image. This is not really a separate modality in the sense used by the cited cross-modal learning work; it is a symbolic target derived from the game engine. The paper may still be about weakly supervised representation learning from automatically generated labels, but the cross-modal framing does not add much and may blur the contribution. The analogy to deep reinforcement learning is similarly only motivational. The experiments do not involve reinforcement learning, sequential decisions, rewards, exploration, or policies. The claim that this helps answer whether a DRL network “understands” game concepts is therefore indirect at best.

Several points need clarification. Are the reported classification and localization results computed on held-out states or on the training set? How are the train, validation, and test splits constructed, and can rotations or reflections of the same board appear across different splits? What is the label generation procedure for states with multiple winning moves, and how many such cases are there? Does the network see only positions where the next move wins, or does it also train on non-winning states? How is the ideal activation map defined for RCO, and why are the reported correlations negative? How sensitive are RAC and RCO to random initialization, crop and rendering details, CAM resolution, and pretraining? Can the learned representation select moves in states that do not end the game immediately, or transfer to a different rendering without retraining?

Overall, I appreciate the simplicity and creativity of the setup, and the observation that CAMs can activate on empty squares is worth reporting in a more focused paper on visualization behavior in synthetic relational domains. The current version, however, makes stronger claims about concept emergence, rule understanding, and cross-modal higher-level semantics than the experiments justify. The task labels already encode the desired action, the evaluation appears limited to a small and possibly non-held-out dataset, and CAM evidence alone is not enough to infer conceptual understanding. My recommendation is rejection in its present form. With rigorous held-out generalization tests, stronger baselines, clearer metrics, causal attribution experiments, and more cautious claims, a revised version could become a useful case study in weakly supervised localization and probing of CNN representations.

text:
The paper proposes a memory-augmented attention architecture for video captioning. Its main idea is to improve standard attention-based sequence-to-sequence models by keeping a recurrent memory of earlier attention decisions while generating a sentence. The model has three parts: a temporal encoder over video frames using convolutional feature maps and location attention, a hierarchical attention and memory module that attends over the encoded frame sequence conditioned on the decoder and memory states, and a recurrent decoder that predicts the next word. The authors evaluate the method on MSVD and Charades and report competitive results, including strong BLEU scores on MSVD without optical flow, C3D features, or fine-tuned action features.

The submission addresses a real weakness in simple video captioning models. A good caption often requires attention to an event that unfolds over time, not just to a single frame or a short local segment, while also keeping track of what has already been described. The proposed architecture is a plausible way to approach this. The separation between frame-level temporal encoding, spatial or location attention within convolutional maps, and a higher-level memory over generated words and attended visual states is sensible. Using convolutional feature maps rather than only fully connected CNN features lets the model attend spatially, and the recurrent memory module could in principle reduce repeated or inconsistent attention during decoding.

Another strength is that the model is trained end to end and does not rely on hand-engineered semantic representations or explicit action labels. That is desirable for captioning, where the goal is to learn the visual-to-language mapping directly. The paper also evaluates on two datasets with different properties. MSVD is a common benchmark with many reference captions, while Charades is more challenging and action-centered, with fewer captions per video. Including Charades is useful because it tests whether the model can handle more realistic activities and less dense language supervision. The qualitative examples also help show where the method succeeds and where it fails.

I have several significant concerns, however, about the technical clarity, novelty, and empirical support for the claims. The first is that the proposed memory mechanism is not explained precisely enough to make its contribution clear. The HAM module is described as storing previous attention and an encoded version of the input videos conditioned on previously generated words. The equations, though, look like a fairly standard recurrent attention mechanism: attention scores are computed from the encoded video states, the previous decoder state, and the previous memory state, and the weighted visual feature is then fed into an LSTM memory. It is not clear in what sense all previous attention distributions are explicitly stored, since the memory seems to be a compressed recurrent hidden state rather than an addressable memory. The paper repeatedly contrasts this approach with “local” attention and says the model can consider the whole video while generating each word, but conventional soft attention over all encoder states already does that. The added recurrent memory may still help, but the conceptual distinction needs to be sharper.

The novelty relative to existing attention and reviewer-style captioning models is also not fully convincing. Conditioning attention on the previous decoder state and earlier contextual information is common in sequence-to-sequence attention models. The paper argues that prior work does not explicitly store all previous attention, but the implementation does not appear to store the full sequence of past attention maps either. It summarizes prior decisions through an LSTM state. This may be a reasonable design, but the paper should be more careful when presenting it as a qualitatively different memory architecture. A stronger discussion would explain whether the benefit comes from adding another recurrent layer between attention and decoding, using convolutional feature maps with spatial attention, conditioning attention on a memory state, or some combination of these factors.

The experiments do not adequately isolate these possibilities. The ablation table is useful, but the results are somewhat confusing and do not support all of the claims. On MSVD, the full HAM+TEM model has the best METEOR among the ablations, but HAM without TEM has better BLEU-2, BLEU-3, and BLEU-4, along with similar CIDEr. The simpler attention model has better CIDEr than the full model. The claim that TEM and HAM complement each other is therefore only partly supported. If the full model is better, that should be shown more consistently across metrics or explained as a tradeoff between metrics. It would also be important to report variance over multiple runs, since the absolute differences are small and could plausibly come from random initialization, frame sampling, or hyperparameter search.

There are also inconsistencies in the experimental setup that make the results harder to interpret. The ablation study uses 40 frames per video, while the main MSVD comparison uses 8 frames per video. This makes it difficult to understand how frame sampling affects the architecture, especially because the temporal encoder is one of the proposed contributions. If temporal modeling is important, the paper should analyze performance as a function of the number of sampled frames. It should also clarify whether hyperparameters were tuned separately for each ablation and baseline, or whether the full model received more tuning. Because the reported hidden sizes are quite large and selected by random search, the fairness of these comparisons matters.

The state-of-the-art claim is overstated. On MSVD, the model has strong BLEU scores among methods that do not use external motion or action features, but it is not best on all metrics. Another method in the table has substantially higher METEOR, and methods using additional features outperform the proposed model on BLEU-4 and METEOR. It would be fair to say that the method is competitive and achieves the best reported BLEU-4 among the listed methods without external features. The broader claim in the abstract and conclusion that it outperforms all previously proposed methods and reaches a new state of the art is not supported by the tables. The Charades results improve on the dataset baseline, but the gain is modest, and the absolute scores remain far below human performance. More analysis is needed before drawing strong conclusions about action understanding.

The paper also lacks several implementation details needed for reproducibility. The frame sampling strategy is not fully specified. The decoding procedure is missing important information, including whether greedy decoding or beam search is used, what beam size is selected, how unknown words are handled, and how maximum caption length is chosen. The preprocessing description mentions NLTK tokenization, but does not describe vocabulary thresholds, handling of rare words, start and end tokens, or whether captions are lowercased. The architecture section gives equations for the main modules, but some dimensions and definitions are unclear, especially in the attention update where repeated decoder and memory states are concatenated or broadcast across frames. The loss function omits the decoder parameters from the listed parameter set. These issues may not be fatal, but they reduce confidence in the empirical results.

The qualitative examples point to another limitation: the model can produce fluent but semantically wrong captions, sometimes hallucinating common objects or actions. This is a known problem in captioning systems, but it matters here because the paper claims that memory-augmented attention improves reasoning over actions and temporal structure. Some incorrect examples suggest that the model may rely heavily on language priors. A stronger evaluation would include attention visualizations over time and space, showing whether the model attends to action-relevant frames when generating verbs and object-relevant regions when generating nouns. Since the central contribution is an attention and memory mechanism, visualizing or quantitatively evaluating its behavior would be valuable.

I have several questions for the authors. In what precise sense does the model store all previous attention decisions, rather than only a recurrent summary of them? Have you compared HAM with a standard attention decoder that has an additional recurrent layer and a comparable parameter count, to rule out the possibility that the gains come from increased capacity? How sensitive are the results to the number of sampled frames, and why are 40 frames used in the ablation while 8 or 16 frames are used in the main experiments? Were the ablation models given the same hyperparameter search budget as the full model? What decoding method and beam size were used for the reported results? Can the authors provide attention visualizations or an analysis showing that the memory state reduces repeated attention or improves verb generation? Can the state-of-the-art claims be revised to reflect the mixed results across metrics and feature settings?

Overall, the direction is promising and the architecture is reasonable, but the submission does not yet meet the level of clarity and empirical rigor I would expect for acceptance. Conditioning video attention on a recurrent memory of prior attended context is a worthwhile idea, and the results are competitive. Still, the novelty over standard recurrent attention mechanisms is not clearly established, the ablations do not convincingly validate the claimed contributions, and some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. My recommendation is rejection in its current form, with encouragement to resubmit after clarifying the memory mechanism, strengthening the baselines and ablations, adding reproducible experimental details, and tempering the performance claims.
